title: 甘蔗养殖技术与效益分析
text:
The cane comes up thigh-high by June, and that’s when I stop sleeping through storms.

I run forty acres outside of Lafourche, though “run” makes it sound like I’m in charge of something. Mostly I walk the rows before the mosquitoes wake up, checking the soil crust, looking for the gray leaf spot, that faint watermark on the blade that tells you the spores beat the spray. My neighbor Ronnie says cane farming is just gambling with mud. He’s not wrong. Last season we put down 8.7 tons of seed cane per acre, billeted by hand because the mechanical cutter kept splintering the nodes, and the stand came in patchy anyway—some variety called LCP 85-384 that the extension agent swore by, but the pH in the lower ten was off by half a point and the tillering never filled in. You learn to live with half-measures.

We plant in fall, late September if the rain lets up. Furrows forty inches apart, seed pieces laid flat, eyes to the side, covered with three inches of dirt. Then comes the waiting. The sugar doesn’t really accumulate until the nights turn cool and the plant panics, shoving everything into the stalk. Before that it’s nitrogen and water, nitrogen and water, and watching the glyphosate bill climb. Fertilizer ran me about $340 an acre this year, custom application included. Weed control another ninety. You can skimp on lime, maybe skip a second cultivation, but if you cheap out on drainage you’ll pay in rot by January.

Drainage is the prayer you repeat. The field has to shed water but hold enough that the roots don’t dry out in October. I put in shallow ditches every sixty feet, shaped like open Vs, and still lost a near-bottom strip to standing water after that tropical depression in late August. Four acres. I walked it after the water receded and the stalks had that sour smell, like wet cardboard and fermentation. We cut them early for seed, ate the loss.

Harvest is where the math gets honest. A good stand yields thirty-two, thirty-five tons to the acre. This year I averaged twenty-eight, which at the mill contract price—roughly thirty-one dollars a gross ton after hauling deductions—puts gross revenue around eight hundred sixty per acre. Subtract rent, fuel, the combine lease, the cost of the seedstock saved from the previous crop, and you’re left with maybe a hundred and forty an acre if nothing else breaks. The nothing-else-breaks part is the fiction.

Still. There’s a morning in late November, after the first real frost, when the whole field goes bronze and the juice runs thick and the cutters start up at the edge of the property, and for an hour or two the arithmetic doesn’t matter. The air smells like crushed cane and diesel and the sweetness is so heavy you can wear it. My daughter came out last harvest before she left for college, stood at the fence in her grandmother’s coat, and said it smelled like burnt sugar. I told her that’s because it is.

Ronnie sold his place to a hunting lease in February. Says he’s tired of owing money to the weather. I think about it sometimes, driving back from the co-op with another pallet of bags in the truck bed, the radio crackling with a forecast I don’t trust. But then the shoots push through again in April, that impossible green against the brown ground, and I start making notes for next year—try a different cultivar on the wet corner, raise the beds another two inches, see if the new slow-release nitrogen is worth the extra cost.

You never really get ahead. You just get another season.

title: 海底两万里
text:
The Garden at the Bottom of the Sea

Professor Pierre Aronnax stood at the observation window of the Nautilus and watched the last pale sunlight melt into the water. Two hundred meters down, the sea had gone almost black, but Nemo's submarine kept sinking without hesitation.

"We're approaching the coral forests of the Torres Strait," Nemo said. His eyes caught the light from the electric lamps. "Brace yourself, Professor. Few men alive have seen what you're about to see."

The Nautilus slipped between two tall cliffs of coral, branches sagging under colors Aronnax had no names for. Fish moved past in silver streams, their scales catching the light. Then the submarine entered a wide underwater valley where the coral had formed shapes like old cathedrals, spires stretching toward a surface they would never reach.

"A graveyard," Nemo whispered.

Aronnax pressed his forehead to the glass. Now he could make out dark shapes among the coral towers—the bones of ships. Wooden ribs stuck up from the sand like the skeleton of some huge animal. Cannon lay scattered around as if a giant had left his toys behind. On one Spanish galleon, the figurehead—a woman carved from oak—stared back at him with blank wooden eyes, her hair wrapped in seaweed.

"How many souls rest here?" Aronnax asked.

"Enough," Nemo said, "to remind me why I chose the sea over mankind."

A shadow moved across the window. At first Aronnax thought it was only ink in the water, but then he saw the octopus coming down from above. Its body was nearly as wide as the Nautilus, and its tentacles stretched longer than any ship's masts above the waves. Each sucker looked as big as a dinner plate. Its eyes held something cold and intelligent, nothing human.

The creature wrapped a tentacle around the submarine. Aronnax felt the metal groan under his feet. Another tentacle hit the glass, and for one terrifying moment he was staring straight into an eye the color of old blood.

"Captain?" he managed.

Nemo stayed where he was. "Watch," he said.

Electric charges crackled from ports along the hull into the water. The octopus shuddered, let go, and drifted back into the darkness, its tentacles trailing after it like the hem of some black dress.

"We don't kill what we don't need to kill," Nemo said quietly. "That's my law down here."

As the Nautilus rose again toward the moonlit surface, Aronnax stayed at the window. He thought about the wooden woman in the coral. He thought about the octopus's ancient eye, and Nemo's law, which seemed both merciful and terrible. He had come aboard this iron ship looking for monsters, he realized. But the truest monsters—and maybe the truest wonders too—were still the ones he carried inside himself.

The sea was patient. It kept all its secrets. For now, it kept Captain Nemo too.

title: 我国农村电商发展现状与对策
text:
Rural E-commerce in China: Where the Platform Ends and the Dirt Road Begins

Abstract

China's rural e-commerce expansion has outpaced its logistical backbone. This paper examines the gap between platform penetration and sustained profitability in county-level agricultural markets. Using provincial statistics and scattered county reports from 2021–2023, we describe three structural bottlenecks: last-mile cost, human capital deficits, and non-standardized output. A hypothetical cost model for a citrus cooperative in Hunan Province illustrates that cold-chain investment only breaks even under narrow assumptions about shipment volume, spoilage reduction, and unpaid family labor. The analysis is bounded to inland counties where road infrastructure is already classified as hard-surface; it does not apply to remote mountainous hamlets lacking all-weather roads. The findings suggest incremental gains in specific corridors, not sweeping rural transformation.

Keywords: rural e-commerce; agricultural value chains; last-mile logistics; digital divide; China

---

1. Chen’s Sweet Potatoes and the Illusion of Volume

Chen sells sweet potatoes from a village in western Hunan. Three hundred kilograms a week. He loads them on a motorbike, rides twelve kilometers to the nearest courier station, and pays rates calculated as if he were a small factory in Guangdong. He makes money. Not much.

This is the reality that aggregate statistics obscure. By 2023, national rural e-commerce transaction volume had crossed the symbolic trillion-yuan threshold. Millions of rural households hold seller accounts on platforms such as Pinduoduo and Douyin. Yet volume is a misleading metric. The relevant question is whether e-commerce raises net farm income after accounting for labor, packaging, logistics, returns, and platform fees. In most inland counties, the answer is: modestly, sometimes, and only under specific conditions.

This paper focuses on agricultural-product e-commerce in counties classified as *rural* by National Bureau of Standards (NBS) definitions. We deliberately exclude suburban exurbs that benefit from metropolitan logistics networks. Our arguments draw primarily on central and southwestern provinces—Hunan, Hubei, Sichuan, Guizhou—where terrain is hilly and agricultural output is dominated by smallholders. The findings may not generalize to the northeastern grain belt or to coastal manufacturing villages that ship non-agricultural goods.

2. Three Hard Constraints

2.1 Logistics: The Cost of Distance and Emptiness

Last-mile costs consume 15–25% of retail price in hilly central China. In the Yangtze Delta, the figure often falls below 8%. The gap is not simply mileage. It is asymmetry. Trucks arrive in villages full of consumer goods for local buyers; they leave mostly empty. Agricultural shipments are seasonal, lumpy, and perishable. A courier station cannot amortize its fixed costs across steady daily volume. 

We assume, for the purposes of later illustration, a roughly circular service area with uniformly distributed villages. Real settlements follow ridge lines and river valleys, so actual routing efficiency is worse than our model implies.

2.2 Human Capital: Training for Clicks, Not for Costs

County governments and platforms have run tens of thousands of digital-skills training sessions. The curriculum typically covers interface operations: how to list a product, how to start a live stream, how to respond to comments. Rarely does it cover inventory depreciation, spoilage accounting, or return-rate negotiation. The result is a dense market of low-margin sellers who compete almost exclusively on price. A household that knows how to broadcast a video but cannot calculate per-unit cost will undercut its own harvest.

We assume that training programs have zero effect on backend management unless they exceed forty hours of instruction and include practicum modules. Most existing programs do not meet this threshold, so we treat their impact as negligible for profitability.

2.3 Standardization: The Apple Problem

E-commerce demands uniformity. A consumer buying apples online expects consistent size, color, and bruise rate. Smallholders cannot supply this without consolidation. Rural cooperatives are the obvious institutional fix, but their governance is often weak. Members free-ride on quality control; sorting and grading equipment sits underutilized.

We treat cooperative consolidation as a black-box efficiency gain in Section 4. We acknowledge that real-world coordination costs—monitoring, enforcement, side-selling—may negate half or more of the projected benefit.

3. Responses That Work, Sometimes

Central-government subsidies for cold-chain construction expanded significantly after 2020. They make sense only where utilization rates are already high. Building a refrigerated warehouse in a village that ships sporadically is capital thrown at a calendar problem. The investment pays off in high-volume corridors with extended harvest windows or multi-crop rotations.

Platform experiments offer another angle. Pinduoduo and others have embedded “agricultural commissioners” in select counties to assist with listing optimization and quality control. Early reports from Hubei and Sichuan suggest a 10–15% revenue bump for participating households. Whether this covers the commissioner’s salary and travel depends on local crop value. The model likely fails for low-margin grains; it may suit citrus, tea, or specialty livestock.

Live streaming has lowered entry barriers. It has not solved exit barriers. A failed live-streaming vendor still faces the same spoilage and return logistics as before.

4. A Hypothetical Cost Illustration (Explicit Assumptions)

To make the arithmetic concrete, we construct a toy model. It is not a regression. It is arithmetic with explicit assumptions, intended to show break-even sensitivity rather than to predict outcomes.

Consider a hypothetical citrus cooperative in a Hunan county. We assume the following:

- Fixed monthly cold-chain depreciation, electricity, and maintenance: 4,200 RMB;
- Average shipping distance to the provincial hub: 280 km;
- Baseline spoilage without cold chain: 18%; with cold chain: 7%;
- Average sale price net of platform commission and packaging: 5.2 RMB/kg;
- Monthly shipment volume: 10,000 kg;
- Labor for cold-chain management is unpaid family labor.

Under these assumptions:

Without cold chain, revenue loss from spoilage equals 0.18 × 10,000 kg × 5.2 RMB/kg = 9,360 RMB.

With cold chain, spoilage loss drops to 0.07 × 10,000 kg × 5.2 RMB/kg = 3,640 RMB.

Gross savings: 5,720 RMB. Minus fixed cost of 4,200 RMB, net monthly gain is 1,520 RMB.

The investment appears positive. Now change two assumptions. First, require hired labor at 2,500 RMB/month to manage the cold store during odd hours. Second, acknowledge that in this region, ice-rain events close mountain roads for a cumulative three weeks per year, forcing spoilage spikes and alternative routing that adds 0.4 RMB/kg. Under these revised assumptions, the monthly ledger turns negative by roughly 1,400 RMB.

The point is narrow. Cold-chain investment is not universally good. It is conditionally good. The condition is high, steady volume plus unpaid or underpaid labor plus reliable road access. Policy makers who fund cold storage without checking these three boxes are subsidizing concrete, not income.

5. Limitations and Scope Boundaries

Every argument here carries geographic limits. The logistics data rely heavily on central and southwestern provinces; northeastern grain belts face different seasonal constraints and bulk-shipping economics. Our hypothetical model is illustrative, not predictive. We did not have access to platform-level transaction microdata; conclusions about profitability rest on aggregated county reports that almost certainly smooth over household-level losses. 

We also assume that platform fee structures remain stable, which they do not. Pinduoduo, Douyin, and Taobao adjust commission and traffic-purchase rules frequently. A shift in algorithmic favoritism can render a county’s dominant sales channel unprofitable within a single quarter.

6. Conclusion

Rural e-commerce in China is no longer a technology problem waiting for a digital solution. It is a coordination problem wrapped in thin margins.

Platform connectivity has solved the first-mile information gap. What remains is the physical movement of irregular, biodegradable goods across difficult terrain at costs that leave growers with net income above subsistence. The plausible gains are incremental: better route consolidation, modest cold-chain additions in high-volume corridors, and training that targets bookkeeping and spoilage control rather than buzzwords.

Anyone promising “rural revitalization through e-commerce” should be required to show the unit economics for a specific crop on a specific road in a specific month. Until then, Chen’s sweet-potato account remains a side hustle. It is not a transformation.

---

References

Chen, X. (2022). Cold-chain investment decisions in smallholder cooperatives: A break-even analysis. *Food Policy*, 112, 102402.

Liu, Y. (2021). Platform penetration in rural counties: Transaction volume versus seller profitability. *Journal of Rural Studies*, 87, 45–58.

Ministry of Commerce. (2023). *Annual report on rural e-commerce development*. Beijing: MOFCOM Press.

Zhang, L., & Wang, H. (2022). Logistics costs and agricultural e-commerce adoption: Evidence from Hubei province. *China Economic Review*, 74, 101823.

Zhao, R. (2023). Digital skills training and household income: Limitations of short-term programs. *China Agricultural Economic Review*, 15(2), 298–315.

title: 一次难忘的旅行
text:
Reflections on "An Unforgettable Trip"

The story in "An Unforgettable Trip" is a simple one. A boy goes hiking with his father, full of energy at the start, and then the trail gets steep. His legs ache. He wants to stop. Halfway up, he nearly turns back. What keeps him going is something his father says: "The most beautiful scenery belongs to those who never give up." So he climbs on, and at the top he watches the sun come up over the mountains. That's the whole plot, really. But it stayed with me.

Honestly, the sunrise wasn't the part I kept thinking about. It was the moment he wanted to quit. I've felt that exact feeling—the embarrassing urge to just sit down on a rock and announce you're done. If he had turned around, the trip would have been nothing, just another Saturday walk nobody remembers. The climb mattered because it cost him something. I'm not even sure the view itself was the real reward; maybe the reward was that he didn't stop.

The essay also made me a little suspicious of how I travel. Most trips I take with my family are basically a checklist: get there, take photos at the famous spot, buy a snack, leave. We did that at West Lake last summer and I can barely recall anything except the crowd. This story suggests the point of a journey isn't the place at all—it's what the road does to you on the way. That sounds dramatic, I know. Still, I think there's something to it, and it applies to school too, where the "mountains" are things like long exams and drills that feel endless.

Reading it brought back my own almost-quitting moment. Last year I signed up for an English speech contest, and by the third week of practice I hated the sound of my own voice. Repeating the same three minutes every night after homework felt pointless. I told my teacher I wanted to drop out; she talked me into one more week. Somehow I stayed. When I finally stood on that stage and got through it without forgetting a line, my hands were shaking—but I was grinning. "No pain, no gain" is printed on posters everywhere and I usually roll my eyes at it. That day, I believed it a little.

So the essay is not really about a mountain. It's a quiet argument that the hard part is the point—that an ordinary hike, or an ordinary month of practice, only turns into something you keep because you nearly gave up on it. I can't say reading it made me brave overnight; I still dread steep stairs. But the next time I want to quit something, this story will probably come back to me. The best views come after the hardest climbs, or so the father in the story claims. I'd like to find out whether he's right.

title: 马铃薯品质提升与增效途径
text:
Title: Pathways to Better Potato Quality and Production Efficiency: An Integrated Review

Authors: Xin Zhang¹, Yue Li¹*, Hao Wang²  
¹ College of Agronomy, Northwest A&F University, Yangling, Shaanxi 712100, China  
² Institute of Vegetables and Flowers, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Beijing 100081, China  

*Corresponding author: Yue Li, email: yli@nwafu.edu.cn

---

Abstract

Potato (*Solanum tuberosum* L.) is among the world’s most important food crops, supplying energy, micronutrients and income to millions of households. Yet as market competition tightens and the climate becomes more erratic, growers increasingly need tubers that combine high yield with strong quality and low production costs. This review brings together current thinking on how to advance both quality and efficiency through an integrated set of strategies: genetic improvement, sound crop management, precision nutrient and water supply, integrated pest and disease control, mechanization, and better postharvest handling and value addition. The literature makes it clear that no single measure is enough. Rather, coordinated adoption of several approaches offers the most dependable route to high-quality tubers, efficient resource use, and sustainable intensification of potato systems.

Keywords: Potato; Tuber quality; Yield efficiency; Integrated crop management; Postharvest; Sustainability

---

1. Introduction

Potato is one of the most widely produced and consumed food crops worldwide (FAO, 2023). It is eaten as a staple and also supplies raw material for chips, French fries, starch and dehydrated flakes. Consumers and processors now look beyond tonnage alone; they want good appearance, nutritional value, processing traits and a smaller environmental footprint (Love & Pavek, 2008).

Quality is usually judged by specific gravity, dry matter and starch content, reducing-sugar levels, flesh color, skin finish, tuber size distribution, and freedom from defects and disease. Production efficiency, meanwhile, is about how well inputs such as seed, water, nutrients, labor and energy are turned into marketable yield and profit. Pushing both quality and efficiency at the same time is difficult, because practices that maximize yield can lower dry matter or alter sugar profiles, while measures aimed mainly at quality may reduce yield. That is why integrated approaches are essential.

2. Genetic Improvement of Quality and Efficiency

Breeding remains the bedrock of potato improvement. Breeders aim for high, stable yields, resistance to major biotic stresses such as late blight (*Phytophthora infestans*), viruses and bacterial wilt, and better tuber quality traits (Bradshaw & Ramsay, 2005). Molecular markers and genomic selection are now widely used to speed up selection for complex traits like starch content, resistance to cold-induced sweetening, and nutritional value (Li et al., 2018). Another promising direction is hybrid breeding built on diploid inbred lines, which can combine heterosis with uniform quality (Lindhout et al., 2011). Widening the genetic base by tapping wild relatives and landraces—many of them conserved at the International Potato Center—also supplies novel alleles for stress tolerance and quality.

3. Soil and Crop Management

Site selection, crop rotation and seed quality set the stage for high-quality potato production. Potatoes do best on well-drained loamy soils with moderate fertility and a pH around 5.0–6.5. Continuous cropping encourages soil-borne diseases and erodes tuber quality, whereas rotations with cereals or legumes reduce pest pressure and improve soil structure (Struik & Wiersema, 1999). Planting certified, disease-free seed tubers of the right physiological age gives uniform emergence and more consistent tuber sizing. Adjusting planting density and date to match cultivar traits and local climate raises marketable yield and cuts the share of undersized or oversized tubers.

4. Nutrient and Water Management

Balanced fertilization matters for both yield and quality. Nitrogen drives vegetative growth, but too much delays maturity, lowers dry matter content and increases disease susceptibility (Zwartz, 1992). Phosphorus and potassium support tuber development, starch accumulation and skin quality. Precision nutrient management—built on soil testing, leaf tissue analysis and growth-stage needs—can trim input costs and environmental losses without sacrificing quality (Davenport et al., 2005).

Water management is equally important. It shapes tuber yield, specific gravity and the incidence of physiological disorders such as hollow heart and growth cracks. Drip irrigation and fertigation allow water and nutrients to be delivered precisely, improving water-use efficiency and tuber uniformity (Shock et al., 1998). Mild deficit irrigation during tuber bulking can raise dry matter concentration, but it must be managed carefully to avoid too large a yield penalty (van Loon, 1986).

5. Integrated Pest and Disease Management

Late blight, viruses, bacterial wilt and nematodes all threaten potato quality and productivity. Integrated pest management brings together resistant cultivars, certified seed, field sanitation, crop rotation, biological control, and targeted pesticide applications guided by decision-support systems (Wale et al., 2008). Cutting back on pesticides lowers production costs and also improves food safety and environmental outcomes. Roguing virus-infected plants and monitoring aphid vectors help keep seed quality and processing suitability high.

6. Mechanization and Precision Agriculture

Mechanization improves labor efficiency and planting uniformity, both of which affect tuber size distribution and harvest losses. Precision agriculture tools—remote sensing, unmanned aerial vehicles, yield monitors and variable-rate applicators—make it possible to manage inputs site-specifically (Haverkort & Verhagen, 2008). Real-time canopy monitoring lets growers act quickly on nutrient deficiencies, water stress or disease outbreaks, protecting both yield and quality.

7. Postharvest Handling and Value Addition

Preserving quality after harvest is just as critical as producing it. Proper curing, careful control of temperature and humidity, and sprout suppression during storage all reduce losses and maintain processing quality (Kirkman, 2007). For processing cultivars, storage temperature has to balance sprout control against cold-induced sweetening, which raises reducing sugars and the risk of acrylamide formation during frying (Haase, 2008).

Processing into chips, fries, flakes, starch and specialty products can greatly improve economic efficiency (Kaur et al., 2007). Developing cultivars for specific end uses and building closer ties between farmers and processors help ensure that quality gains translate into higher income.

8. Conclusion

Improving potato quality and production efficiency calls for a systems-level approach. Genetic improvement sets the biological potential; agronomic, nutritional, water and pest management practices unlock it in the field. Mechanization and precision agriculture raise input-use efficiency, while postharvest innovation preserves quality and adds value. Future potato production systems should weave these strategies into a broader sustainability framework, balancing productivity, profitability, food quality and environmental stewardship.

---

References

Davenport, J. R., Milburn, P. H., Rosen, C. J., & Thornton, R. E. (2005). Nutrient management. In: *Potato Production Systems* (pp. 167–183). The Scientific World.

title: The Hedgerow
text:
Phased Implementation Checklist for The Hedgerow

*Assumption: This checklist assumes The Hedgerow is a 60–80 seat farm-to-table restaurant and bar with a garden built around a hedgerow theme, seasonal menus, botanical cocktails, and a strong preference for ingredients from nearby farms and growers. If your actual concept differs—smaller, larger, no garden, or a different menu style—tell me and I’ll rework the list.*

This is a working checklist, not a guarantee. Timelines slip. Prices change. Adjust as you go.

---

 Phase 0 — Concept & Feasibility (Weeks 1–4)

| Step | What to do | Who owns it | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | Write the brand brief in one page: “farm hedgerow,” botanical ingredients, hyper-local sourcing, seasonal cooking, and hospitality that tries to leave the soil better than you found it. | Founder + Creative Director | One-page brand brief signed off |
| 0.2 | Map the service model by daypart: weekday lunch, dinner nightly, weekend brunch, bar-only hours, a private dining nook, and occasional events. | GM + Founder | Service model matrix |
| 0.3 | Set rough targets for covers, average check, and revenue by daypart. Your first pro-forma will be wrong. Update it weekly. | Finance + GM | Pro-forma P&L v1 approved |
| 0.4 | Visit three to five possible sites with real outdoor or garden space; measure foot traffic at different times, count parking spaces, and list permit constraints. | Founder + Real Estate | Site comparison scorecard |
| 0.5 | Walk the competition inside a three-mile radius; note what they charge, how busy they are, and where the gaps are. | Marketing + GM | Competitor SWOT |
| 0.6 | Talk to at least fifty prospective guests or run a small local focus group before you lock in prices. | Marketing + Chef | Pricing validation report |
| 0.7 | Lock in funding and set aside a six-month operating reserve, not a three-month one. | Finance + Founder | Funding memo signed |

Go/No-Go Gate: Do not sign the lease until the brand story, site, and funding line up.

---

 Phase 1 — Business Foundation & Site (Weeks 4–12)

| Step | What to do | Who owns it | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | Sign the lease or purchase agreement only after confirming the building can handle the kitchen load: electrical service, HVAC, grease-trap size, and exhaust capacity. | Founder + Attorney | Executed lease |
| 1.2 | Form the LLC or corporation and buy insurance that actually covers a restaurant: general liability, liquor liability, workers’ comp, and property. | Attorney + Finance | Insurance certificates |
| 1.3 | File for the liquor license, food-service permit, sign permits, outdoor-dining permit, and music licenses from ASCAP, BMI, and SESAC. | GM + Attorney | Filed applications + tracking log |
| 1.4 | Hire an architect and interior designer who have already done restaurants, not just houses. | Founder | Signed contracts |
| 1.5 | Lock the floor plan: roughly 60 dining-room seats, 12 bar stools, 20 garden seats, a small private dining nook, and a clear ADA path from door to restroom. | Architect + GM | Approved construction drawings |
| 1.6 | Build a real budget covering construction, furniture/fixtures/equipment, opening inventory, pre-opening payroll, and marketing. | Finance + GM | Approved budget |
| 1.7 | Choose a general contractor and schedule weekly walk-throughs. | Founder + GM | Construction contract + schedule |
| 1.8 | Open business checking and set up the books in QuickBooks, Xero, or whatever your accountant prefers. | Finance | Chart of accounts live |
| 1.9 | Buy the domain, grab the social handles, and file the trademark for “The Hedgerow” before someone else does. | Marketing | Digital assets secured |

Go/No-Go Gate: Permits are submitted, the budget is approved, and the contractor is under contract.

---

 Phase 2 — Design, Build & Systems (Weeks 10–22)

| Step | What to do | Who owns it | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | Finalize the design package: natural wood, a living green wall, hedgerow planting, and mismatched vintage glassware. | Designer + Founder | Final design package |
| 2.2 | Order the long-lead pieces first: custom bar, banquettes, pendant lighting, patio furniture, and a decent sound system. | GM + Designer | POs + delivery schedule |
| 2.3 | Build out the line: a ten-burner range, combi ovens, a walk-in cooler, prep stations, dish pit, and a corner for pastry. | Chef + Contractor | Equipment list installed |
| 2.4 | Install the bar backbone: ice maker, draft lines, speed rails, back-bar shelving, and a glass washer that can keep up. | Bar Manager + Contractor | Bar spec signed off |
| 2.5 | Set up the garden: pollinator-friendly plants, edible herbs, drip irrigation, patio heaters, and string or path lighting. | Facilities + Landscaper | Garden ready for seating |
| 2.6 | Pick and contract the tech stack: a POS such as Toast, reservations through Resy or SevenRooms, inventory in Marketman or similar, payroll through Gusto or your accountant’s pick, and scheduling in 7shifts. | GM + Finance | Signed tech contracts |
| 2.7 | Run Wi-Fi that reaches the garden, install security cameras, wire the music system, and add backup power for the POS. | IT + Facilities | Systems live and tested |
| 2.8 | Launch a simple website: menu placeholder, reservations link, an “our story” page, and basic accessibility compliance. | Marketing | Website launched |
| 2.9 | Pass rough inspections for plumbing, electrical, fire, and health. | Contractor + GM | Inspection sign-offs |
| 2.10 | Order and install signage: an exterior blade sign, window vinyl, wayfinding inside, and a small garden-rules sign. | Marketing + Designer | Signage installed |

Go/No-Go Gate: Buildout is substantially complete, the technology is live, and the final health inspection is scheduled.

---

 Phase 3 — Menu, Beverage & Supply Chain (Weeks 14–20)

| Step | What to do | Who owns it | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | Write the opening seasonal menu—four starters, four mains, three sides, two desserts—and cost every dish to hit roughly 28–32% food cost. | Chef | Opening menu + costing sheet |
| 3.2 | Build an allergen matrix and simple dietary symbols: vegan, gluten-free, dairy-free, nut-free. | Chef + Sous | Allergen chart posted |
| 3.3 | Write recipe cards with photos, yields, plating notes, and par levels; keep them where the line can actually read them. | Chef + Sous | Recipe binder or digital playbook |
| 3.4 | Curate the botanical cocktail list: eight signatures, four zero-proof options, four twists on classics; target 18–22% pour cost. | Bar Manager | Cocktail spec sheets |

title: 大豆高产栽培技术要点
text:
Soybeans look easy from the road. They are not.

Getting a high yield starts with picking the right variety. You cannot plant a Group V bean up north and expect it to finish before frost. Check the maturity group for your county. Also look at disease packages. If you have soybean cyst nematode in your fields, and plenty of people do without knowing it, plant a resistant variety. The seed bag should say SCN resistance. If it does not, keep looking.

Soil matters more than people think. Soybeans tolerate a lot, but they do not like wet feet. Tile drainage helps if you have heavy clay. Get a soil test. pH should sit around 6.5. If you are down at 5.8, fix that first with lime. Do not skip it. Phosphorus and potassium need to be adequate, especially potassium. Low K shows up later as yellow edges on the leaves and then you are already losing beans.

Planting depth is three quarters of an inch to one and a half inches. An inch is usually right. If you plant too shallow in dry soil, the seed coats crack but the root does not push down. Too deep and the hypocotyl runs out of energy before it sees sunlight. Use a seed treatment if the soil is cool. Fungicide on the seed buys you two weeks of protection against damping off.

Inoculate the seed if you have not grown beans in that field for three years. Bradyrhizobium bacteria form the nodules. Some farmers skip this to save eight dollars an acre and then wonder why the plants stay yellow. It is cheap insurance. Pour the inoculant on right before planting if it is a peat-based product. Liquid works too but does not stick as long in dry conditions.

Population depends on row width. In fifteen-inch rows, plant around 140 to 150 thousand seeds per acre. In thirty-inch rows, bump it to 160 thousand because you lose more to gaps. Narrow rows close the canopy faster and choke out weeds. That matters because soybeans do not compete well early. Waterhemp and pigweed will take over if you let them.

Weed control starts clean. Burn down with glyphosate or paraquat before planting if there is green vegetation. Then pre-emerge with metribuzin or whatever fits your rotation. Do not let weeds get six inches tall before you spray. By then the damage is done. The bean plants know they are being shaded. They stall.

Nitrogen fertilizer is usually not needed if nodulation is good. Some farmers put on twenty or thirty units anyway as starter. It can help in sandy soils or if nodulation fails. Do not go heavy. Too much nitrogen makes the plant lazy. It stops fixing its own and you get big vines with few pods.

Scout for insects in July and August. Bean leaf beetles chew holes in the leaves. Aphids cluster on the stems and upper leaves. If you have fifty aphids per plant and they are increasing, spray. Watch for podworm too, especially if you are near corn. They bore into the pod and eat the seed. One worm per plant does not sound like much but it adds up across forty acres.

White mold is a problem in tight rotations and thick canopies. You see it when the weather turns cool and wet during flowering. There are fungicides that help if you time them right at R1 or R3. But honestly, the best control is wider rows and not overdoing the water.

Harvest at thirteen to fifteen percent moisture if you can. Below thirteen, you are losing weight to cracked beans and dockage. Above fifteen, you pay drying charges or risk storage mold. Check the stems. When most pods are tan and the leaves have dropped, it is time. Do not wait for every last pod. The late ones will be green and hard. They will go out the back of the combine.

Get your combine settings right. Too fast and you crack them. Too slow and you leave beans in the field. Open the concave a bit. Start there.

That's about it. The beans mostly grow themselves after planting. But the part before planting, and the few decisions right after, that is where the bushels come from. Miss one detail and you still get a crop. Miss three and you are below average again.

title: 田野与四季
text:
The Wisdom of the Fields: Lessons from the Four Seasons

Step into a supermarket in December and you'll find strawberries stacked high under fluorescent light while the world outside sits frozen. Climate-controlled rooms and year-round everything have let modern life stop paying attention to the seasons, but the fields never got that option. They green up in spring, ripen through summer, give up their bounty in autumn, and then sleep under the frost—which makes them one of the last honest calendars we've got. And that turning cycle is more than a nice view. It's a teacher, I'd argue, with lessons about work, patience, and rest that a society like ours can't afford to keep ignoring.

Start with spring and summer. A farmer plows and sows with zero guarantee of return; it's basically an act of faith that a seed dropped into cold dirt will somehow turn into standing grain. Summer then asks for something less dramatic but harder—persistence. The weeding and watering drag on through the heat, and from one day to the next the crops barely seem to change at all. That's the field's answer to our fantasy of instant results. Nothing worth harvesting shows up overnight. Every golden ear of wheat is really just months of unglamorous labor made visible. If you're looking for an argument against the culture of one-click delivery and overnight success, a wheat field in July makes it better than any book could.

Autumn and winter teach different lessons, but no smaller ones. In autumn, the long effort of the earlier months is finally answered with abundance—the harvest is nature's proof that patience isn't naive. Winter, though, might be the most radical teacher of the four. A fallow field lying under snow looks idle, but that stillness is preparation, not laziness. Soil that's allowed to rest builds its fertility back; a field pushed to produce without pause wears out quickly. We happen to live in a culture that glorifies nonstop productivity and quietly files rest under weakness. The winter field pushes back on that, gently but firmly: nothing renews itself without first stopping for a while.

Now, you might object that humanity has simply outgrown the seasons. Greenhouses, refrigeration, and global supply chains do let us eat tomatoes in January and work at one unbroken pace all year. Fair enough. But that freedom carries costs we rarely add up. Pushing the land to ignore its own rhythms strains the soil and, ultimately, the climate. On the cultural side, our drift away from seasonal time has coincided with record burnout and a fading sense of where food even comes from. We gained convenience, sure—but we lost a framework that used to teach people how to wait, how to work, and, just as importantly, how to stop.

So the fields are much more than scenery on a country drive. They're a philosophy written in soil and weather. Spring is hope and the nerve to begin; summer is hanging on; autumn is gratitude; winter is the dignity of rest. Walk the same fields across a single year and you get an education in time itself—one no screen can give you. If we want lives that are more grounded and more sustainable, we could do worse than return, at least in spirit, to that old classroom of the fields and relearn what the four seasons have been saying all along.

title: 短视频对大学生的影响
text:
The Impact of Short-Form Video on College Students: A Double-Edged Sword

Author Name  
*Department of Psychology / Media Studies, University Name*  
*Corresponding email: author@university.edu*

---

Abstract

Short-form video platforms—TikTok and its Chinese counterpart Douyin, Kuaishou, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts—have moved from niche entertainment to daily habit for large numbers of college students. A clip can last anywhere from a few seconds to a few minutes, and the feed refreshes endlessly, pulling users through breakfast, commutes, and late-night scrolling. These applications fit the fragmented schedules of undergraduates: a quick break between lectures easily becomes twenty minutes. Yet the same design that makes short-form video engaging also raises real worries about concentration, procrastination, and anxiety.

This paper offers a narrative review and theoretical analysis of how short-form video use affects college students. It draws on uses and gratifications theory, variable-ratio reinforcement, and cognitive load theory to argue that these platforms can support informal learning and weak-tie socializing while also encouraging compulsive checking and attention fragmentation. The effects are neither uniform nor fully causal. Patterns of use matter, as do individual self-control and campus context. Balanced use, better media literacy, and targeted institutional support appear important, though more longitudinal research is needed to say exactly which interventions work best.

Keywords: short-form video; college students; academic performance; mental health; media literacy

---

1. Introduction

Short-form video means audiovisual content made for quick, mobile consumption: usually seconds to a few minutes, easy to swipe through, and easy to share. TikTok went global in 2018; Douyin launched in China in 2016; Instagram added Reels in 2020 and YouTube rolled out Shorts in 2021. Together these services now claim billions of users. College students, who live with smartphones in hand and move between lectures, part-time jobs, and shared housing, make up a large slice of that audience. For many, short-form video is entertainment, news, background noise, and sometimes a substitute for textbooks.

The design is persuasive. Autoplay removes the pause between clips. Algorithms learn preferences fast. The next video might be forgettable, or it might be the one that makes a user laugh aloud in the library. That unpredictability keeps people returning. So while these platforms open doors to knowledge and connection, they also make sustained attention harder. Educators, counselors, and policymakers need a clear-eyed picture of both sides. This paper tries to provide one.

---

2. Theoretical Framework

2.1 Uses and Gratifications Theory

Uses and gratifications theory treats audiences as active choosers who pick media to meet specific needs: information, diversion, companionship, identity work. Short-form video is unusually versatile in this respect. A student might open the app to learn a single Excel shortcut, then stay for a parody of campus life, then reply to a comment from someone in another province. The same feed satisfies curiosity, boredom, and the wish to belong. That multi-use quality helps explain why usage can spike during transitions such as freshman year or exam periods.

2.2 Variable-Ratio Reinforcement and Cognitive Load

Behaviorally, the feed resembles a variable-ratio reinforcement schedule. The reward—an amusing, useful, or shocking clip—arrives unpredictably. Users keep swiping because the next one might be great. Behavioral psychologists have long known that intermittent rewards sustain behavior longer than predictable ones.

Cognitively, rapid switching between unrelated clips taxes working memory. A student who has spent an hour jumping from cooking hacks to political commentary to dance trends may find it harder to settle into a dense journal article. The transition cost is real, though it varies across individuals and tasks.

---

3. Positive Impacts of Short-Form Video

3.1 Informal Learning and Skill Acquisition

Short-form video has become a genuinely useful informal educational tool. A student can watch a 90-second explanation of a Python error, a two-minute breakdown of a historical event, or a 45-second pronunciation tip. Compared with a two-hour lecture, these clips feel low risk. They can spark interest in topics outside a formal major or help someone review a concept before an exam.

Still, quality is uneven. A viral tip may be oversimplified or flat wrong. A one-minute clip can introduce an idea, but it rarely builds deep skill. Students who rely on short-form video as a primary learning source may overestimate how much they understand.

3.2 Social Connection and Emotional Regulation

For students far from home or still building campus friendships, these platforms can reduce isolation. Commenting on a niche interest, joining a trend, or following a creator who shares the same major can create a sense of belonging. Humorous clips also offer quick stress relief. A funny cat video after a difficult midterm is not a cure-all, but it can reset mood briefly.

Yet the social ties formed this way are often thin. Likes and follows are not the same as face-to-face support. Some students may spend hours curating an online persona while feeling lonely in a dorm room full of people.

---

4. Negative Impacts of Short-Form Video

4.1 Attention Fragmentation and Academic Procrastination

The most common criticism is that short-form video fragments attention. Clips are short by definition, the interface is fast, and rewards are immediate. Students may grow less patient with slower, more demanding material. Montag, Yang, and Elhai (2021) argue that TikTok’s design features encourage habitual checking and pull users away from responsibilities.

The result is often procrastination. Reading assignments get postponed. Problem sets stretch late into the night. Causality is hard to pin down, because students who already struggle with self-regulation may also be drawn to highly stimulating apps. Still, the correlation between heavy use and lower study efficiency shows up often enough to be taken seriously.

4.2 Problematic Use and Mental Health

Problematic short-form video use looks in some ways like a behavioral addiction: preoccupation, tolerance, withdrawal when offline, and difficulty cutting back. Kuss and Griffiths (2011) note that online social networking becomes addictive when it fills needs such as escapism and validation. Short-form video platforms do exactly this, with public metrics—likes, views, follower counts—that can intensify social comparison.

Students may feel anxious if a post underperforms, or if they see peers whose lives look more exciting than their own. Excessive use has been linked to depressed mood, loneliness, and poor sleep. Again, these are mostly correlational findings. Not every heavy user becomes distressed. But the pattern is strong enough that campus counseling centers now routinely hear about social-media-related anxiety.

4.3 Information Cocoons and Misinformation

Recommendation algorithms tend to show users more of what they already watch. A student who clicks on one fitness video may soon see dozens more, often from a narrow slice of opinion. Over time this can create an information cocoon that limits exposure to disagreement or complexity.

Short-form format also strips context. A 30-second clip can spread a misleading health claim, a polarizing political take, or a simplistic reading of a scientific study before anyone has checked the source. Nuance is hard to fit in. The problem is not unique to short video, but the speed and shareability make correction difficult.

---

5. Discussion

The effects of short-form video on college students depend heavily on how, when, and why students use it. Someone who watches a five-minute coding tutorial during lunch is having a different experience from someone who mindlessly scrolls until 2 a.m. before an exam. Intentionality and context matter at least as much as total screen time.

Universities can respond without treating all app use as a moral failure. Orientation programs can include short, practical units on how recommendation algorithms work and how to set app timers. Counseling services can screen for problematic use when students report anxiety or sleep trouble. Faculty might also acknowledge that students learn from many sources, then help them evaluate which ones are trustworthy.

Platform designers bear responsibility too. Autoplay can be turned off by default. Screen-time reminders can be more intrusive. Metrics could be hidden or de-emphasized. These changes would not eliminate harm, but they would support user autonomy rather than treating attention as a resource to be extracted.

---

6. Conclusion and Recommendations

Short-form video is now woven into college life. It can teach, connect, and entertain. It can also distract, isolate, and mislead. Neither praise nor panic captures the full picture.

Students can take small steps. Disable autoplay. Set a timer. Ask whether a session is productive or merely automatic. Institutions can strengthen media literacy and make mental-health support easy to find. Researchers should keep tracking long-term outcomes across cultures, because most of the evidence so far is cross-sectional and comes from a handful of countries.

The challenge is not to eliminate short-form video, which is unlikely, but to help students use it on their own terms. That balance is possible. It is also unfinished.

---

References

Andreassen, C. S., & Pallesen, S. (2014). Social network site addiction—An overview. *Current Pharmaceutical Design, 20*(25), 4053–4061.

Kuss, D. J., & Griffiths, M. D. (2011). Online social networking and addiction—A review of the psychological literature. *International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 8*(9), 3528–3552.

Montag, C., Yang, H., & Elhai, J. D. (2021). On the psychology of TikTok use: A first glimpse from empirical findings. *Frontiers in Public Health, 9*, 641673.

Su, C., Zhou, H., Gong, L., & Zhang, Y. (2021). Why users continue to use short-form video applications: The role of gratification, habit, and problematic use. *Behaviour & Information Technology, 40*(16), 1–15.

title: 读书的意义
text:
The Uses of Reading: What Books Can and Cannot Do

Abstract

Claims about reading often outrun the evidence. This paper examines the significance of reading book-length texts in three areas: cognitive development, social understanding, and the formation of an inner life. Throughout, I assume that “reading” means sustained, voluntary engagement with extended prose, whether print or digital, and I deliberately exclude skimming, compulsory school assignments, and short-form screen media. The argument is that reading can improve vocabulary, deepen perspective-taking, and support attention, but these effects are modest, genre-dependent, and contingent on how a person reads. Reading is neither a moral guarantee nor a universal remedy. Its value is practical and plural, and it matters most when it is chosen, reflected upon, and connected to life outside the page.

Keywords

reading, literature, cognitive development, empathy, attention, print culture

---

 1. Introduction

People have been praising books for millennia. They have also burned them. Both reactions suggest that reading matters, but neither tells us exactly how.

This paper asks a narrower question: what can reading book-length texts plausibly do for an individual, and where do common claims overreach? I will not try to cover every genre, every culture, or every medium. My scope is limited to voluntary, sustained reading of extended texts—novels, histories, essays, biographies, and similar works—in contemporary literate societies. I treat “book” loosely; a long PDF or e-reader file counts if it demands the same continuous attention as a bound volume. I do not treat scrolling through news feeds, watching video adaptations, or reading under heavy external coercion as the same activity, because the psychological processes involved are different.

My central claim is modest. Reading is one practice among many that can shape how we think, feel, and relate to others. It is not uniquely transformative, and its benefits are easy to exaggerate. The sections that follow state their assumptions explicitly and mark illustrative cases as hypothetical, so the reader can see where the evidence ends and speculation begins.

---

 2. Reading as a Cognitive Practice

One of the least controversial effects of reading is exposure to language. Someone who reads complex prose regularly encounters more words, more syntactic structures, and more extended arguments than someone who does not. Over time, this exposure can widen vocabulary and improve the ability to follow intricate sentences.

That sounds straightforward. It is also easy to overstate.

The assumption behind this claim is that the reader is paying attention and occasionally encountering unfamiliar words. Passive decoding—moving the eyes across the page while thinking about dinner—does little. So does reading only very simple texts. The cognitive benefit is therefore a function of both the difficulty of the book and the engagement of the reader.

Hypothetical example. Imagine two adults of similar age and education. One reads literary fiction for thirty minutes each evening; the other spends the same time browsing short posts and comments online. After a year, the fiction reader would likely score higher on a vocabulary test. But we cannot conclude from this that fiction *causes* the difference. The fiction reader may already have had a larger vocabulary, more free time, or stronger verbal interests. The comparison is useful as a heuristic, not as proof.

There is also evidence that sustained reading can train attention. Books ask the reader to hold a narrative or argument across dozens or hundreds of pages. This is different from the rapid reward cycles of much digital media. Whether that training generalizes to other tasks is less clear. Some studies suggest a link between leisure reading and longer attention spans; others find the effect disappears once education and socioeconomic status are controlled. I therefore treat “reading improves attention” as plausible but not established.

---

 3. Reading, Empathy, and Social Understanding

A more debated claim is that reading—especially literary fiction—makes us more empathetic. The idea has an intuitive appeal. Fiction puts us inside other minds, other eras, other social worlds. By following characters whose circumstances differ from our own, we may become better at inferring what other people think and feel.

Kidd and Castano’s widely cited 2013 study reported that reading literary fiction, but not popular fiction or nonfiction, briefly improved performance on theory-of-mind tasks. Later replication attempts produced mixed results. Some failed to find the effect; others found it only under specific conditions. The debate is not settled, and it would be dishonest to present the original finding as settled science.

The assumption I am making here is that empathy is not a single skill that any story automatically strengthens. It depends on the quality of the text, the disposition of the reader, and the nature of the engagement. A novel that flattens its characters into stereotypes may confirm prejudice rather than reduce it. A reader who consumes a tragic story purely for plot may feel little for the people in it.

Hypothetical example. Consider a reader who finishes a novel about a refugee family forced to leave their home. If she pauses to imagine their fear and uncertainty, she may become more attuned to similar experiences in real life. But if she treats the book merely as entertainment and forgets it within days, or if the novel presents the family as helpless victims without agency, the effect on her everyday attitudes may be negligible—or even negative.

The scope of this argument is also limited. Most studies measure short-term changes in laboratory tasks, not long-term moral behavior. Knowing how someone feels is not the same as acting on that knowledge. Reading might make a person more understanding; it will not make her kind if she does not want to be.

---

 4. Reading and the Inner Life

Not all value of reading is instrumental. Some of it has to do with what it feels like to read.

Reading creates a particular kind of solitude. The body is still, but the mind is active. For a time, the reader is neither fully in the world nor fully absent from it. This middle state can be restful, especially in environments saturated with noise, notifications, and demands for immediate response.

Here I am assuming a certain social condition: the reader has enough quiet, enough time, and enough safety to read voluntarily. That assumption does not hold for everyone. A parent working two jobs, a student in an overcrowded household, or a person living through war may not experience reading as refuge. So when I say reading can sustain an inner life, I mean it can do so under conditions that already permit some privacy and leisure.

There is also a pleasure specific to language itself: the rhythm of a sentence, the surprise of a metaphor, the satisfaction of a well-placed word. Roland Barthes called this the “pleasure of the text.” That pleasure is real, but it is not universal. Some readers find it in poetry; others in technical manuals; others not at all. There is no single inner life that reading necessarily produces.

---

 5. Civic and Social Dimensions

Reading can also have public significance. Shared books create shared references. When many people in a society have read the same novels, histories, or essays, they have a common vocabulary for discussing values, memories, and possible futures. Libraries, book clubs, and literary festivals are among the institutions that sustain this kind of public culture.

The assumption here is that there is some overlap in what people read. In practice, that overlap has shrunk. Print culture is fragmented. Algorithms push different texts to different readers, and national “canons” are increasingly contested. A book that one group treats as essential, another group may never have heard of. So the civic function of reading depends on whether a society still cultivates spaces where diverse readers encounter the same works.

Moreover, access is uneven. Wealth, schooling, geography, and language all determine who gets to read what. Celebrating reading as a civic good can obscure these inequalities. Reading matters socially only when it is widely and equitably available.

---

 6. What Reading Does Not Do

It is worth stating the limits plainly, because much popular writing about books drifts into sentimentality.

Reading does not automatically make a person good. Intelligent, well-read people have committed terrible acts. Reading does not replace action. Knowing about injustice is not the same as opposing it. Reading does not guarantee happiness or mental health; for some, it is an escape that postpones necessary confrontation with real problems. And reading is not a magic defense against misinformation: bad books, conspiracy texts, and propaganda are still books.

These limits do not mean reading is worthless. They mean its value is conditional. It depends on what is read, how it is read, and what the reader does with it afterward.

---

 7. Conclusion

Reading is significant, but its significance is not singular.

Under the right conditions—voluntary engagement, sufficient difficulty, reflective attention, and access to varied texts—reading can expand vocabulary, sharpen the ability to understand other minds, and provide a rare form of quiet absorption. It can also contribute to a shared culture, though that contribution is fragile and uneven.

These effects are modest, not miraculous. Reading will not save democracy, cure loneliness, or turn a selfish person into a saint. The evidence for many of its benefits is suggestive rather than conclusive, and much depends on the reader.

What remains valuable, even so, is the practice itself: the act of slowing down, following someone else’s language across time, and allowing one’s own thoughts to be shaped by words not originally one’s own. That experience is not available only through books, but books have long been one of the most reliable places to find it. The meaning of reading is not that it changes everything. It is that, sometimes, it changes enough.

---

 References

Bauerlein, M. (2008). *The Dumbest Generation: How the Digital Age Stupefies Young Americans and Jeopardizes Our Future*. Tarcher/Penguin.
