title: 柑橘水肥一体化技术应用
text:
The soil between the rows used to crack like old leather. You’d dump the granular urea by hand, white crystals catching in your boots, and pray the afternoon thunderstorm didn’t wash it all down to the creek before the roots could find it. That was the deal. Money in the dirt, then hope.

Now the ground stays this strange, even color. Dark brown, damp but not muddy, the way a sponge holds water right before it drips. I walked the Valencia block at six this morning, coffee going cold in my hand, listening to the pump house hum three hundred yards off. It’s a low sound, almost like bees in a wall. The fertigation rig kicked in at five-fifteen. Nitrogen and a shot of potassium, metered out through the injectors, mixed into water that already ran clean from the well. 

I knelt by Tree 47. The drip line lay curled against the trunk like a tired snake, each emitter releasing a slow, pulseless bead. No fanfare. Just chemistry and gravity doing their quiet business. The feeder roots, I know, have started branching toward the moisture. They always do. Smart, in their dumb way.

Marta hates that I still call it “the new system,” even though we installed the manifolds three winters ago. But I remember the old tanker truck. I remember the dust. My hands still carry the memory of those fifty-pound bags, the cuts on the palms, the way the fertilizer burned if sweat got into the scratches. Now I adjust a dial in the pump house, watch the Venturi injector pull the concentrate down a clear tube, and that’s the ceremony.

There was a clog last Tuesday. Calcium buildup in an emitter near the fence line. I found it because the leaves on that one tree looked pale, almost yellow at the veins, while its neighbors flushed deep green. That’s the thing—when you feed slow and steady, the trees become gossips. They tell on each other. One starves, and you see it immediately. Before, with broadcast feeding, a whole row could go hungry and you wouldn’t know until the fruit set small and bitter.

The sun’s up now, burning off the last of the valley fog. I can smell the citrus coming, that sharp green oil smell that clings to your clothes. A drop of the fertigated water hangs from the lowest leaf on Tree 47, fat as a pearl. It catches the light. I don’t touch it. There’s no need. The tree already drank exactly what it needed, and the rest is just gravity, finishing the sentence.

I head back toward the pump house. The motor changes pitch, dropping an octave as the cycle ends. Somewhere in the lines, the pressure equalizes. The grove goes quiet, except for a mockingbird in the windbreak who doesn’t care about efficiency one way or the other.

title: 乡村的变化
text:
The Village Remembers: Reflections on a Changing Countryside

When I think of the village where I grew up, I picture it in watercolor — the edges soft, the colors faded, everything stuck at that gray-blue hour just before sunrise. Mist used to rise off the rice paddies, slow and steady, as if the fields were breathing in their sleep. Nobody needed an alarm clock. The roosters took care of that, along with the groan of oxcart wheels and the wet slap of laundry being beaten against the river stones. At night there were stars — more than you'd believe — because electricity was still just a rumor from the town, and the dark was the real thing, thick and total.

Back then, life kept time with the seasons, not the clock. Spring meant the whole family ankle-deep in cold water, pushing rice seedlings into the mud in rows my father insisted be straight enough to satisfy a schoolteacher. Summer was cicadas going all day and us kids splashing in the irrigation ditches until somebody's mother yelled. Come autumn the paddies turned gold. And winter — winter was slow. Nets got mended, stories got told and retold around the fire, and mostly we waited. We were poor, there's no getting around that. But the village made sense on its own terms. It had a completeness to it, its own quiet dignity.

The changes snuck up on us. A telephone line appeared one year, a stretch of paved road the next. Then all at once it was like the spring thaw — everything happening faster than anyone could keep track of. I'll never forget the evening the lights first came on in every house. The whole village glowed like a ship that had been drifting in the dark for years and somehow, against all odds, found its harbor.

These days the village looks like a different place entirely. The muddy tracks I remember are gone, covered over by concrete roads smooth as river stones. The old tiled cottages have mostly come down, replaced by houses two and three stories tall, their walls glaring white in the sun. Grandmothers who used to holler across the fields now video-call their grandkids in far-off cities, their weathered faces lit up by phone screens. In the square, tourists snap photos of the restored ancestral hall, hoping to catch some of the authenticity that progress has scrubbed out of everywhere else. Whether they actually find it is another question.

I'd be lying if I said nothing was lost. Nobody sings the old songs anymore. The loom in the corner hasn't moved in years. The river where I learned to swim runs shallow now, and no one washes clothes along its banks. Some nights, walking through the village, I catch myself missing the darkness we used to have — that enormous sky drunk on stars, now washed pale by the glow of streetlamps.

But grief is only half of it, and I'd be telling the story wrong if I stopped there. I've watched old farmers, finally spared the worst of the backbreaking labor by small machines, sit out in the afternoon sun with actual time on their hands — time to play chess, to laugh. There's a young woman who came back from the city and now sells her family's honey through livestreaming to customers a thousand miles away, and the funny thing is, her village accent — the thing people used to be embarrassed about — is exactly what sells. Kids who a generation ago would have left school at twelve are talking about university now. None of this is small. It's the difference, I think, between a life you endure and a life you actually live.

Maybe the countryside works like a river. The water is never the same twice, yet somehow it's always the same river. The soul of the village was never really in the kerosene lamps or the dirt roads. It's in tougher, more durable stuff — neighbors still showing up with baskets of whatever they've harvested, the whole village still turning out for weddings and funerals, the land still feeding and grounding the people who work it.

Near dusk I climb the hill above the village and watch the new lights flick on, one after another. From up there, past and present sit side by side like layers of sediment — the old stone bridge right next to the new concrete one, the ancestral graves looking down on a field of solar panels. The village has changed. It's changing still, and I doubt it will stop. But as the first stars come out — the same ones that hung over my childhood — it occurs to me that some things hold underneath all of it: the seasons turning, the sowing and the harvest, and the old human longing, whatever era you happen to be born into, to belong to a place and call it home.

title: 小麦品质提升与增效途径
text:
My grandfather believed wheat quality came from suffering. Dry springs, thin soil, a frost right at flowering—that was his recipe for hard kernels and bread that held together. He wasn’t entirely wrong. Stress can pack protein tight. But stress is also a gamble. Some years you get empty heads and grain so shriveled the elevator just shrugs. I spent twenty years learning the difference between useful struggle and stupid waste.

On the farm I took over from him, I work the other way around.

Better variety first. We stopped planting whatever seed the co-op had left over in October. Took three seasons testing eight cultivars on the south forty, the piece with the calcareous subsoil that always shows you who’s honest. We kept two. One has strong gluten for the mill. The other yields heavier, but still hits twelve percent protein if you nurse it. The seed costs more. The first year I winced writing the check. The second year the elevator paid a premium and I stopped wincing.

Soil is where the real laziness happens. I used to think tillage was work. Turns out it’s mostly moving dirt around to feel busy. We switched to no-till on the heavier fields and strip-till where the wind cuts through. Left the stubble standing. The earthworms came back like they’d been waiting for an invitation. Organic matter crept from 1.2 to near 2 percent in seven years. Doesn’t sound like much unless you’re the one watching water soak in instead of running off. Roots go deeper. The plants don’t yellow so fast when May turns hot.

Nitrogen is the trickiest. Too little, protein drops and the baker complains. Too much, lodging and a bill you can’t pay. We split applications now. A little at planting, more at tillering, the last shot at flag leaf based on a chlorophyll meter reading my daughter treats like a video game score. Variable-rate from drone maps. Still learning. Last season I held back thirty kilograms on the east plot and the grain tested the same. Saved money. Smaller footprint. The words sound clean; the field looked no different, which is exactly the point.

Water we manage like we’re rationing wine. Drip on the seed corn, but wheat gets sprinkler only if it must, never flood. Timing matters more than volume. One good irrigation at jointing beats three sloppy ones later. The roots do the searching. You want them searching, not bathing.

Disease is simpler now that I walk more and spray less. I scout the lower canopy in the morning when dew still holds. Rust shows up orange and arrogant. Fusarium, that quiet thief, comes after a wet flowering. We plant resistant varieties, rotate with canola, and only pull the fungicide out when the threshold says so. The grain comes in cleaner. Anyone who has lost a truck to vomitoxin discounts knows what I mean. I lost one once. Never again.

Harvest is patience dressed up as machinery. Cut at thirteen percent moisture, not eighteen, no matter how tired you are and how dark the clouds look. Green kernels in the bin will heat. A night in a hot silo can undo a year.

This morning I stood at the edge of the south forty. The wheat was still green at the base, turning the color of old brass on top. Wind made it move like water. I rubbed a head between my palms and blew the chaff away. The kernels were small still, hard as baby teeth. My grandfather would have said they were suffering beautifully. Maybe. But at least this time they weren’t suffering for nothing.

title: 傲慢与偏见
text:
A Practical Step-by-Step Guide to Reading and Enjoying *Pride and Prejudice*

1. Choose the right edition  
   Start by grabbing a solid, well-annotated edition—Penguin Classics and Norton Critical Editions are both good bets. The footnotes really matter here, since they clear up old-fashioned language, inheritance laws, and the social rules that shape almost every scene.

2. Learn the historical context  
   The novel is set in Regency-era England, roughly the early 1800s. Marriage back then wasn’t just about love; it was tightly bound up with money, social rank, and family expectations. Entailment laws also meant estates usually passed only to male relatives, which is why who inherits what becomes such a big deal.

3. Get familiar with the main characters  
   Elizabeth Bennet is sharp, funny, and quick to judge; Mr. Darcy comes off as proud and standoffish but turns out to have a strong moral core. Jane and Bingley give us the sweet, almost idealized romance, while characters like Mr. Collins, Lady Catherine de Bourgh, and Wickham stand in for social absurdity, manipulation, and real danger.

4. Track the relationships and misunderstandings  
   Much of the plot hinges on Elizabeth reading Darcy wrong. Wickham’s lies and Darcy’s own cold manner don’t help. Over time, though, Darcy shows genuine humility through what he does rather than what he says. Meanwhile, Jane and Bingley’s relationship shows how outside interference can nearly ruin a good match.

5. Read for Austen’s irony and wit  
   Don’t just race through the story. Pause at the famous opening line—“It is a truth universally acknowledged…”—and watch how Austen reveals people through their conversations and small telling details rather than long descriptions.

6. Identify the major themes  
   A few big ideas run throughout the novel: pride and humility, prejudice and first impressions, class and money, marriage and reputation, morality, and the weight of family and social expectations.

7. Focus on key scenes  
   Some moments are especially worth watching for: the Meryton Assembly, where everyone first sizes up Darcy; Elizabeth’s visit to Rosings and her tense encounter with Lady Catherine; Darcy’s awkward first proposal and Elizabeth’s furious rejection; the letter where Darcy finally explains Wickham’s past; Lydia’s elopement and Darcy’s quiet rescue; and the final proposal at Pemberley.

8. Keep a vocabulary and quote notebook  
   Jot down unfamiliar Regency-era words as you go, and copy out lines that stick with you. Those notes will come in handy later, whether you’re writing an essay or just joining a discussion.

9. Reflect on modern relevance  
   After finishing the book, ask yourself how first impressions still shape your own relationships, and whether pride and prejudice continue to influence how people judge one another today.

10. Discuss or write about the novel  
    Talking about the book with others—whether in a club, class, or online forum—almost always brings out new angles. You might also try writing a short essay on how Elizabeth and Darcy each change, or compare the novel with one of its many film adaptations.

11. Revisit the novel later  
    *Pride and Prejudice* tends to reward a second read. Once you know how everything turns out, you’ll catch details and layers of craft you probably missed the first time around.

Quick tip: Slow down during the dialogue scenes. A huge amount of the humor, tension, and character growth happens right there in conversation.

title: 葡萄标准化生产技术
text:
Standardized Production Techniques for Grape Cultivation: A Comprehensive Framework for Quality and Efficiency

Abstract

Grape growers worldwide are under mounting pressure to deliver consistent products, ensure food safety, and keep their operations sustainable—especially as market demands climb and weather patterns become harder to predict. Standardized production techniques offer a practical way to bring more uniformity to farming practices, cut back on chemical use, and lift overall fruit quality across vineyard operations. This review covers the full spectrum of standardized protocols for both table and wine grapes, weaving together varietal selection, site-specific vineyard design, precision water and nutrient management, integrated pest and disease control, and post-harvest logistics. By pulling together recent developments in horticultural science and quality management, we outline a practical framework that connects Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) with precision viticulture. Our analysis shows that adopting standardized operating procedures (SOPs) leads to noticeably more uniform grapes, slashes pesticide residues by 30–45%, and boosts economic returns through smarter resource use. These results make a strong case for moving away from traditional empirical farming toward technology-driven, protocol-based viticulture if the industry wants to stay competitive and environmentally responsible over the long haul.

Keywords: grape production; standardization; integrated pest management; precision viticulture; quality control; Good Agricultural Practices

---

1. Introduction

Grapes (*Vitis vinifera* L. and related species) rank among the world’s most valuable fruit crops, with annual production topping 77 million metric tons across a wide range of agro-ecological settings (OIV, 2023). Yet the industry grapples with no shortage of obstacles: fragmented farm sizes, uneven fruit quality, heavy reliance on agrochemicals, and labor costs that keep climbing. Traditional cultivation tends to lean heavily on experiential knowledge, which naturally leads to significant variation in yield, sugar-acid balance, and safety profiles from one producer—or season—to the next.

To tackle these problems, standardized production technology—essentially the creation and rollout of scientifically grounded, measurable, and repeatable technical specs across the entire production chain—has been gaining real traction. Standardization goes beyond simply unifying operational steps; it also folds in modern tools like soil-sensor networks, decision support systems, and blockchain-enabled traceability. The end goals are straightforward enough: achieve more consistent product quality, shrink environmental footprints, and meet the strict standards demanded by international markets.

In this paper, we break down the core elements of standardized grape production. We look at what happens before planting, including cultivar selection and terroir zoning; the standardized cultural practices used during vegetative and reproductive growth; integrated crop protection protocols; and the standardized workflows for harvesting and post-harvest handling. By working through these technical building blocks, we hope to give viticultural operations a useful reference point for modernization.

---

2. Standardized Pre-Planting and Vineyard Establishment

2.1 Varietal Selection and Regional Adaptation

Getting standardization right starts before planting, specifically by matching cultivar traits to local climate and soil conditions. Wine grape varieties like Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay need particular heat accumulation (degree-days) and wide diurnal temperature swings, while table grape cultivars such as Thompson Seedless, Kyoho, and Shine Muscat are chosen more for their cluster architecture, skin durability, and shelf-life potential. Standardized production also requires certified virus-free nursery stock that meets national or international phytosanitary standards (for instance, OIV descriptor lists) so genetic purity is preserved and pathogens stay out of the vineyard.

2.2 Site Preparation and Soil Standardization

Consistent soil preparation lays the groundwork for an even vineyard. Standard protocols call for thorough soil profiling down to 100 cm to evaluate texture, pH, organic matter levels, and cation exchange capacity. With these data in hand, growers can apply targeted corrections—subsoil ripping to 60 cm where needed, customized lime or sulfur amendments, and organic compost worked in at set rates (usually 15–30 t/ha). Row orientation, vine spacing, and trellis design are then planned around mechanization needs and the desired canopy microclimate.

---

3. Standardized Cultural Management Practices

3.1 Precision Irrigation and Fertigation

Standardizing water management means using evapotranspiration (ET) models and soil moisture sensor networks to guide irrigation decisions, often through deliberate deficit regimes. For premium wine grapes, regulated deficit irrigation (RDI) is typically introduced at veraison to concentrate flavors and keep yields in check. Fertigation schedules deliver macronutrients (N, P, K) and micronutrients (Fe, Zn, B) through drip systems timed to specific phenological stages, with foliar feeding triggered only when tissue analysis shows it is needed. Compared with old-school broadcast applications, this precision approach can cut fertilizer leaching by 25–40%.

3.2 Standardized Pruning and Canopy Management

During dormancy, pruning crews set bud numbers according to established formulas—commonly 8–12 buds per kilogram of pruned cane weight—to strike a balance between vegetative vigor and crop load. Once the growing season begins, standardized canopy management steps like shoot positioning, leaf removal, and cluster thinning help optimize light interception, air movement, and spray penetration. Basal leaf removal around flowering, done to a consistent standard, improves resistance to bunch rot and can boost anthocyanin buildup in red varieties.

---

4. Standardized Pest and Disease Management

4.1 Integrated Pest Management (IPM) Protocols

Rather than spraying on a fixed calendar, standardized crop protection relies on decision-support tools built around economic injury levels (EILs) and phenological forecasting. Growers monitor key pests such as *Lobesia botrana* and *Planococcus ficus*, along with pathogens like *Botrytis cinerea* and *Plasmopara viticola*, using pheromone traps and weather-driven infection models. When sprays are needed, the protocol favors selective products, enforces strict pre-harvest intervals (PHIs), and requires buffer zones so residues stay within Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs).

4.2 Biological and Ecological Control

Biocontrol agents such as *Trichoderma harzianum* and *Bacillus subtilis*, together with habitat management strategies like cover cropping to support parasitoid populations, are deployed according to set release rates and timing. This approach to ecological intensification typically reduces synthetic fungicide use by 30–50% without sacrificing disease control.

---

5. Standardized Harvesting and Post-Harvest Handling

5.1 Maturity Indexing and Harvest Protocols

Deciding when to pick comes down to measurable maturity benchmarks: total soluble solids (TSS, °Brix), titratable acidity (TA), pH, and phenolic maturity for wine grapes, or berry firmness and color for table grapes. Whether harvesting by machine or by hand, crews follow strict protocols to limit bruising. Containers are standardized to avoid compression damage, and field heat is removed quickly by moving fruit straight to pre-cooling facilities.

5.2 Post-Harvest Standardization

For table grapes, SO₂ generator pads, steady cold-chain maintenance at 0–1 °C, and modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) all work to extend shelf-life and keep clusters looking fresh. Traceability codes applied during packing allow full backward tracking to the specific vineyard block, harvest date, and cultural inputs used.

---

6. Quality Control and Certification Systems

Quality Management Systems such as GlobalGAP, HACCP, and ISO 22000 serve to formalize these production standards and embed them in day-to-day operations. Internal audits, standard operating procedures (SOPs) recorded in field logbooks, and digital agriculture platforms all help ensure people actually follow the protocols. Training and certifying workers remains critical, since human operations are still one of the biggest sources of variability in the vineyard.

---

7. Conclusion

Moving toward standardized production marks a fundamental shift for the grape industry, bridging the gap between traditional viticulture and the demands of modern agribusiness. Bringing together standardized site selection, precision inputs, IPM-based crop protection, and rigorous post-harvest protocols demonstrably improves fruit quality consistency, reduces environmental harm, and opens doors to broader market access. Looking ahead, research should explore how artificial intelligence and IoT devices can digitize standard operating procedures to enable real-time monitoring and adaptive management in the field.

title: 夏洛的网
text:
Charlotte’s Web: A Timeless Story of Friendship and Sacrifice

*Charlotte’s Web*, E. B. White’s 1952 novel, still sits on countless classroom shelves and bedside tables across the United States. It follows Wilbur, a runt piglet spared at the start by Fern Arable, a farmer’s daughter who talks her father out of the axe. Later, when Wilbur faces a much larger threat—the autumn smokehouse—his rescue comes from an unexpected source: Charlotte, a gray spider living in the corner of the Zuckerman barn.

The bond between the pig and the spider carries the book. Wilbur is young, anxious, and desperate to live. Charlotte is patient and steady, with a dry humor that keeps the barn from feeling too grim. When she learns the Zuckermans’ plans for Wilbur, she promises to find a way to keep him alive. She spends her nights spinning words into the web above his crate—“Some Pig,” then “Terrific,” later “Radiant,” and finally “Humble”—each phrase a small engineering feat written in silk. Neighbors begin to visit. The county fair crowd gathers. Wilbur’s life becomes valuable because people suddenly believe he matters.

The real weight of the story, though, is not the miracle. It is what Charlotte spends to make it happen. Spinning those messages drains her. By the time Wilbur wins his medal at the fair, Charlotte has no strength left to leave her web. She dies alone at the fairgrounds, leaving only an egg sac behind. Wilbur, who once hid from danger, now guards the sac through the winter and welcomes her children in the spring. That change—from a frightened animal to someone willing to protect another life—makes the friendship feel earned rather than sentimental.

White never lectures. Still, the novel raises hard questions. It asks what friendship actually costs, and whether loyalty can outlast death. It also refuses to pretend that nature is kind; death arrives in plain daylight, without apology. Charlotte’s acts are tiny, almost invisible, yet they redirect the whole course of Wilbur’s life. The book suggests that small creatures matter, and that small gestures can sometimes be enough.

*Charlotte’s Web* ends on a quiet note, neither fully happy nor simply sad. The reader loses Charlotte, but sees her legacy carried forward in the spiders who return to the barn. The story admits that growing up means accepting loss. It also holds onto the thought that the care we offer each other leaves a mark longer than we do.

title: 乡村振兴背景下农民增收路径
text:
Pathways to Boosting Farmers' Income under Rural Revitalization: Mechanisms, Challenges, and Policy Implications

Abstract

China’s Rural Revitalization Strategy now serves as the main policy framework for tackling the country’s “three rural issues”—agriculture, rural areas, and farmers. While the strategy pursues several goals, raising farmers’ income is still the most basic way to judge whether it is working. Drawing on the sustainable livelihoods framework and the “four-wheel drive” theory of rural household income, this study uses a systematic literature review together with a multi-case analysis to explore how farmers can achieve lasting income growth. Our findings suggest that boosting income effectively requires five key mechanisms to work together. First, farmers need to optimize agriculture internally through industrial integration and value-chain upgrading. Second, rural e-commerce and the digital economy can open new revenue streams. Third, rural tourism and service sectors offer additional earning opportunities. Fourth, institutional innovation in land and property rights can lift property income. And fifth, investing in human capital and shifting toward local employment can raise wage income. We also argue that simply transferring resources into rural areas is not enough. Without institutional reform, digital infrastructure, and a strong social safety net, endogenous growth potential cannot fully emerge. The paper closes with practical policy recommendations for creating a multi-dimensional, regionally adaptive income growth system.

Keywords: Rural revitalization; Farmers’ income; Agricultural industrial integration; Rural e-commerce; Land institutional reform; Sustainable livelihoods

---

1. Introduction

China has experienced decades of rapid growth, yet the income gap between cities and villages remains a stubborn structural problem. National Bureau of Statistics data show that while the urban-to-rural disposable income ratio has fallen from its peak, the absolute monetary gap is still growing. The Rural Revitalization Strategy (RRS), formally introduced at the 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, responds to this reality with a comprehensive blueprint that moves beyond the earlier narrow focus on poverty alleviation. It covers industrial, talent, cultural, ecological, and organizational revitalization. Still, no matter how these dimensions are framed, their success ultimately boils down to one measurable question: are farmers’ incomes rising in a sustainable and fair way?

Researchers have long broken down farmers’ income growth into wages, business operations, property, and transfers. However, most existing work looks at just one channel—land transfers or migrant labor, for example—or stays at the macro-regional level without linking specific policies to what actually happens inside rural households. This study tries to bridge that gap by building an integrated framework that connects the macro-level RRS policy design with mid-level industrial change and household-level livelihood choices. More concretely, we ask three questions. What are the main pathways for farmers to earn more under the RRS? Which institutional and market conditions help or block these pathways? And what policy mixes work best when different income strategies reinforce each other?

The rest of the paper is laid out as follows. We begin by reviewing the literature on rural income growth theories, then explain our analytical framework and methods. After that, we systematically examine five core income pathways, discuss how they interact and what obstacles they face, and finally draw out the policy implications.

---

2. Literature Review

2.1 Theoretical Foundations of Rural Income Growth

Classical development economics, especially Lewis’s dual-sector model (Lewis, 1954), argued that moving labor from agriculture to industry would eventually balance marginal productivity and incomes across sectors. Todaro (1969) added a twist by factoring in the probability of actually finding urban work, noting that migration can become irrational when expected city wages look higher than rural earnings. These theories still help explain why migrant labor historically mattered so much for Chinese farmers’ wage income, yet they do not capture why local entrepreneurship and property rights income matter today.

Later, DFID’s sustainable livelihoods framework (1999) turned scholars’ attention toward the “asset pentagon”—human, natural, financial, physical, and social capital. Here, income growth is not just about labor moving out; it hinges on how households draw on and convert their assets when policies or markets shift. This view fits the RRS well, since the strategy deliberately seeks to strengthen all five types of capital at once.

2.2 Empirical Studies on Farmers’ Income in China

Recent empirical work has paid growing attention to structural diversification. Huang and Rozelle (2018), for instance, showed that adopting new farm technologies lifts operating income, but only if villages also invest in market infrastructure. Zhang et al. (2020) discovered that rural e-commerce can close the urban–rural income divide by cutting information gaps and transaction costs. Separately, Lin et al. (2021) confirmed that formalizing land rights and making transfers easier raise both property income and operating efficiency by allowing larger-scale management.

Yet researchers increasingly agree that piecemeal fixes are not enough. Wang and Liu (2022) made the case that industrial integration—blending farming with processing, logistics, and tourism—creates multiplier effects no single-sector push can match. Chen (2023) added that human capital serves as a gatekeeper: without skilled workers, neither digital commerce nor high-value agriculture produces the returns expected. Taking these points together, we treat farmers’ income growth as a systemic result that demands coordination across several pathways.

---

3. Theoretical Framework and Methodology

3.1 Analytical Framework

We use a modified “four-wheel drive” framework combined with the SLF. The four wheels map onto the official components of rural household income—what households earn from operations, wages, property, and transfers. But we do not treat these as separate bookkeeping items. Instead, we examine them as dynamic livelihood strategies that evolve under the influence of policy institutions, market structures, and the assets households already hold (conceptually illustrated in Figure 1).

3.2 Methodology

Because our question is conceptual and policy-oriented, we rely on a qualitative approach that mixes a systematic literature review (SLR) with a multi-case synthesis. The SLR draws on peer-reviewed articles, policy white papers, and statistical yearbooks from 2015 to 2024, sourced from CNKI, Web of Science, and government databases. For the multi-case component, we pull together evidence from several representative regions: Zhejiang, where e-commerce and rural tourism have taken off; Sichuan, known for land reform and industrial integration; and Shandong, which has pushed modern agriculture and cooperative models. These cases help show how each pathway plays out in different local contexts.

---

4. Pathways to Farmers’ Income Growth under the RRS

4.1 Pathway I: Agricultural Internal Optimization and Industrial Integration

The first pathway is the most traditional one: raising the operating income that comes directly from farming. Under the RRS, this no longer means simply producing more grain. Instead, the emphasis has shifted to supply-side structural reform and vertical integration along the agricultural value chain.

title: 失败是成功之母
text:
Failure Is the Mother of Success

A Pastoral Meditation

There is a small plot of earth behind my cottage, scarce twenty paces square if I pace it generously, which I have the vanity to style my garden. Hither, in the spring of the year before last, I carried a quantity of seeds — sweet-peas, hollyhocks, and I know not what beside — and committed them to the soil with as much ceremony as if I had been founding a colony. I pictured to myself, with all the fondness of an expectant parent, the glory that should presently arise from that brown and unpromising bed. Summer came. The sun performed his office faithfully enough; the rains, though something parsimonious, were not altogether wanting. Yet of all my sanguine sowing there arose but three languid stalks — three, out of a whole spring's scheming — and these a company of snails, possessing more appetite than ceremony, despatched in a single night. Their silver trails were still there at breakfast-time, owning to the deed.

I confess I was disheartened, more than the loss of a few seedlings strictly warranted. I was standing one morning in rueful contemplation of my desolation when old Thomas, my neighbour, whose garden is the admiration of the whole parish (and not, I think, entirely against his will), looked over the hedge and enquired the cause of my melancholy. Having acquainted him with my calamity, I observed him smile in that quiet manner of men who have passed threescore summers among growing things; and, leaning upon his spade, he delivered himself thus:

"Why, sir, d'ye suppose yonder cabbages sprang full-grown from Fortune's lap the first season I took a spade in hand? I have buried more failures in this ground than ever I carried cabbages to market. Every gardener keeps two gardens — the one you see, and the one that lies buried beneath it, made up of all his blunders and disappointments; and it is the buried garden, sir, that feeds the living one."

I have often revolved this homely wisdom in my mind since, and the longer I observe the economy of Nature, the more plainly I perceive that she is herself the most patient of all failures. Consider the great oak by the churchyard wall: how many thousand acorns hath she scattered upon the indifferent earth — to be devoured by swine, to perish on the stony path, or to rot, unmissed, in the ditch — ere one fortunate seedling found its appointed soil? The very hedgerows in May are prodigal of blossoms that shall never ripen into fruit. The thrush builds and builds again, though yesternight's tempest strewed her cunning fabric upon the grass. Nature, methinks, keeps no ledger of her defeats; she converts them all, by a divine chemistry, into the very mould her victories are sown in.

The husbandman understands this truth in his bones, though he may never utter it in so many words. He commits his wheat to the autumn furrow not in any certainty of harvest, but in a sort of faithful defiance of disappointment; and should the mildew take it, or the flood, or the untimely frost, he is to be found next season at the selfsame furrow, with the same seed-basket and an unaltered heart. There is in this annual wager against calamity a quiet heroism which the townsman, who buys his loaf without once reflecting on the drama of its making, little suspects. I never suspected it myself, before my three stalks.

Nor is the lesson confined to these western fields. The sages of Cathay, who of all peoples have longest studied the patient husbandry of Nature, are said to have compressed the whole philosophy of endeavour into a single homely sentence — that failure is the mother of success. A plain saying, truly; yet like most plain things, a crust of bread or a draught of spring-water, it carries within it a kernel of immortality.

For my own part, I returned to my little plot the following spring, instructed in humility and furnished with the fruits of my defeat; which is to say, I knew now what not to do — and this knowledge, being purchased at first hand, is the only sort that truly takes root. I dug deeper. I chose my seeds with less ambition and, I flatter myself, more judgment. The sky I studied with the deference due to a capricious sovereign, which is to say I consulted it every morning and believed none of it. And when at length the first green spears broke the ground, I was conscious of a pleasure far exceeding aught I had anticipated in my former ignorance. Success that comes unearned is like fruit dropped from another man's tree — sweet, but with a borrowed sweetness. The harvest reared upon one's own failures, long laboured for and dearly bought, hath in it a savour that is all our own.

So let no man be ashamed of his withered seedlings or his blighted hopes. The soil is enriched by every plant that dies upon it. And the skill of the gardener is nothing, really, but his former blunders — well rotted down and dug under — from which his later triumphs draw their quiet nourishment.

---

title: 生猪产业发展现状与对策
text:
Current Development Status and Countermeasures of the Pig Industry  
*(生猪产业发展现状与对策)*

Author: [Your Name]  
Affiliation: [Your Institution]  
Date: [Month Year]

---

Abstract

In many countries, and above all in China, the pig industry underpins both animal husbandry and the security of meat supplies. After the devastating impact of African swine fever (ASF) and the long rebound that followed, the sector has moved into a different phase—one defined by larger-scale operations, faster technology uptake, and tighter environmental rules. Still, sustainable growth is far from assured. Recurring disease threats, swings in feed grain prices, environmental limits, and sharp market cycles all keep the pressure on. This paper surveys where the pig industry stands today, pinpoints the most pressing problems, and sets out practical responses spanning biosecurity, scaling and standardization, green production, breeding innovation, feed supply security, market stabilization, and downstream processing. The goal is to offer useful guidance for policymakers, companies, and farmers who are trying to steer the industry onto a more sustainable path.

Keywords: pig industry; development status; challenges; countermeasures; sustainable development

---

1. Introduction

Pork ranks among the world’s most important sources of animal protein. In China it dominates meat consumption, so the pig industry matters deeply for national food security, rural jobs, and overall economic stability. Over the last ten years the sector has gone through rapid expansion, structural change, and severe external shocks, most notably the ASF outbreak that began in 2018. Production capacity has mostly bounced back, yet uncertainty lingers around disease control, resource costs, environmental sustainability, and farm profitability. Understanding the current state of the industry and crafting effective responses is therefore critical if the pig sector is to develop in a stable, high-quality, and durable way.

---

2. Current Development Status

2.1 Production Recovery and Supply Security

The collapse triggered by ASF has been followed by a notable recovery, supported by government policies, restocking drives, and capacity expansion. Sow inventories and slaughter numbers have settled back into a more stable range, and the security of pork supply has improved. Measures such as production subsidies, insurance support, and guarantees on land use have been instrumental in keeping the market on an even keel.

2.2 Scale and Structural Adjustment

A clear shift is underway from backyard pig farming toward larger, more standardized operations. Big enterprises are claiming a growing share of total output, helped by economies of scale, better access to capital, and more robust biosecurity systems. This restructuring has lifted production efficiency, strengthened quality control, and made supply more reliable.

2.3 Technological Progress and Breeding Improvement

Modern pig production is becoming increasingly technology-intensive. Automated feeding, climate control systems, data-based herd management, and artificial insemination are now widely used. Some leading firms have also poured resources into genetic improvement, aiming for better reproductive rates, feed conversion efficiency, and disease resistance.

2.4 Green Development and Environmental Compliance

Rules on manure handling, odor control, and water pollution have grown much stricter. Many large farms have turned to resource-recycling models—biogas plants and organic fertilizer processing, for example—converting livestock waste into inputs for crop farming and cutting pollution in the process.

---

3. Main Problems and Challenges

3.1 Recurring Animal Disease Risks

ASF remains a stubborn threat even after the recovery, while other diseases such as porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome (PRRS) and foot-and-mouth disease continue to inflict losses. Small and medium-sized farms often do not have the biosecurity infrastructure to match larger operations, leaving them exposed when outbreaks occur.

3.2 Feed Cost and Resource Constraints

Feed makes up a large slice of pig production costs. Volatility in global grain and soybean markets, together with heavy reliance on imported protein feed, squeezes farm margins. Land and water availability also place real constraints on expansion in certain regions.

3.3 Market Fluctuations and Profitability

Pork prices follow pronounced cycles, which translate into sharp swings in farm income. When prices drop, small producers are often the first to leave the market, undermining supply stability. Ordinary farmers also have limited access to risk-hedging tools, which only makes the income roller-coaster worse.

3.4 Environmental and Land Pressures

Progress has been made, but manure treatment and odor control are still serious headaches, especially in densely populated farming belts. Land-use restrictions and conflicts between livestock farms and nearby residential areas continue to stand in the way of better industry planning.

3.5 Weaknesses in Independent Breeding and Downstream Processing

China still depends partly on imported high-performance breeding stock. Homegrown breeding capacity and the conservation of indigenous pig breeds both need a boost. At the same time, deep processing, cold-chain logistics, and branded pork products are not developing fast enough to keep up with consumer demands for quality and safety.

---

4. Countermeasures and Policy Recommendations

4.1 Strengthen Disease Prevention and Biosecurity

Governments and companies should work together to build integrated systems for disease monitoring, early warning, and emergency response. Large farms ought to enforce strict all-in/all-out management, thorough disinfection routines, and regional biosafety barriers. Smaller farms, meanwhile, need technical guidance and practical support to upgrade their facilities.

4.2 Accelerate Scale and Standardization

Policy should encourage farming at a moderate scale and promote integrated chains that link breeding, fattening, slaughtering, and processing. Standardized practices can raise efficiency, improve traceability and food safety, and lower environmental risks at the same time.

4.3 Improve Feed Efficiency and Grain Supply

The industry should push for precision feeding, alternative protein sources, and more localized feed production so as to reduce dependence on imported soybeans. Strategic grain reserves and well-functioning market regulation mechanisms can also help keep feed costs from spiraling.

4.4 Promote Green Circular Production

Farms should adopt manure-to-biogas, manure-to-fertilizer, and crop-livestock integration models. Incentives for investment in green technologies, backed by firmer enforcement of environmental standards, can move the sector toward genuinely sustainable development.

4.5 Enhance Breeding Innovation and Indigenous Breed Protection

More resources should go into pig genetics research, molecular breeding techniques, and the conservation of indigenous breeds. A stronger domestic breeding system would cut reliance on imported genetics and improve the industry’s long-term resilience.

4.6 Improve Market Stabilization Mechanisms

Governments need to refine pork reserve systems, price monitoring, and early-warning indicators. Wider coverage of agricultural insurance and greater participation in futures markets can give farmers better tools for managing price risk and smoothing out income fluctuations.

4.7 Develop Processing, Cold Chain, and Branding

Support for slaughtering, cold-chain logistics, and processed pork products can add value, cut waste, and cater to increasingly diverse consumer tastes. Building brands around quality, safety, and origin can also sharpen market competitiveness.

---

5. Conclusion

The pig industry has come a long way in recovering production, scaling up operations, adopting new technologies, and embracing greener practices. Even so, disease risks, feed costs, market volatility, environmental pressures, and gaps in breeding and processing continue to block the path forward. Tackling these issues will require coordinated action from government, enterprises, and farmers, with a focus on biosecurity, standardized scale production, green circular models, feed security, breeding innovation, market stabilization, and downstream value-chain growth. Only by pursuing these strategies in an integrated way can the pig industry achieve the kind of stable, high-quality, and lasting growth it needs.

title: 感恩父母
text:
Sometimes I forget they were young once. I look at the photos on the fridge—my mother in a denim jacket, hair feathered back, grinning like she owned the world; my father holding a motorcycle helmet, squinting into the sun—and it feels like a trick. These people had lives before me. Dreams that got smaller.

I remember one winter in middle school. The bus came late, always late, and I stood there hating the cold, hating my coat, hating the fact that we lived far enough from everything that the mornings started in the dark. My father would wait with me. He never said much. Just stood a few feet away, coffee in a chipped mug, breath clouding under the streetlight. I thought it was embarrassing. Now I can’t think of it without my throat tightening. He wasn’t guarding me from danger; the neighborhood was safe enough. He was just there. That’s the part that gets me. He chose to be cold.

My mother used to cut fruit at ten o’clock at night. Apples, pears, whatever was softening in the bowl. She’d bring it to the couch while I did homework and leave the plate without asking if I wanted it. I never thanked her. It was just a thing that happened, like gravity. A few years ago I tried doing it myself—sliced a mango badly, juice running down my wrist—and suddenly I understood the small arithmetic of love: the buying, the washing, the waiting for the right ripeness, the quiet walk down the hall, the not needing credit.

I didn’t become grateful all at once. It came in pieces. The first time I paid rent. The first time I got sick alone and there was no one to bring soup. The first time I called home and heard how glad they were, how quickly they dropped everything, and I realized I had taken that gladness for granted my whole life.

Last month I went back to visit. My father’s hands shook a little when he poured tea. My mother asked me three times if I was eating enough. I wanted to say something big, something that would finally balance the scales, but the words stayed stuck. So I fixed the sticky drawer in the kitchen. I sat through a variety show I didn’t care about. I ate all the fruit.

It isn’t enough. It will never be enough. But I’m learning that love, the kind they gave me, doesn’t keep score. It just keeps showing up.

title: 茶叶水肥一体化技术应用
text:
The Little Tea Leaf and the Magic Straws

Once upon a time, on the soft and often fog-shrouded slopes of Misty Peak, a dense stand of tea plants clung to the hillside. Their leaves were thick and waxy, dark green after the rains. Among them, barely larger than a thumbnail, huddled a tiny bud named Bao. He dreamed of height. Strength mattered too. Mostly, though, he wanted to steep in porcelain and warm the hands of someone who needed it. Maybe a tired traveler. Or a grandmother. He hadn't decided yet.

Growing up, as it turned out, took real effort.

Old Master Chen climbed the slope each dawn with wooden buckets sloshing against his legs. *Splash!* The water came down hard on some plants. *Drip...* barely a trickle for others. When feeding time arrived, Chen scattered the fertilizer by hand from above. The granules were sharp. They tickled. To Bao, the sensation stung like chili flakes in a broth that had already been seasoned once too many. *"Cough, cough,"* he'd whisper when no one else was listening. *"This isn't right. Not for me."*

That summer the heat settled early. The clay soil cracked in places. Bao's leaves curled at the edges, losing their spring snap. He flagged down a ladybug who was resting on a nearby stem.

*"I'm thirsty,"* Bao admitted. His voice was small. *"My stomach, if buds can be said to have stomachs, feels empty. I keep thinking—what if the water came to me? Right here. At my feet. Gently."* The ladybug had no answer. She simply adjusted her spotted wings and flew off toward shade.

One Tuesday evening, or perhaps it was Wednesday—Bao lost track—Master Chen returned. He carried coils of pale blue tubing, the kind made from recycled rubber, soft as old t-shirts. He knelt beside Bao with knees that popped softly and worked one end of a tube into the earth. It stopped a thumb's width from Bao's thinnest root hair.

*"Magic straws,"* Chen called them, though he smiled in a way that suggested he knew better. *"Science straws, really. Science is the magic we can explain."*

The tubes ran uphill to a drum, a battered green barrel Chen had patched with aluminum tape. Inside sloshed a mixture he had tested three times that morning. The salinity was low. He had measured the nutrients with a chipped plastic spoon. Nothing would fall from the sky this time. Everything would arrive from below, where roots could take it or leave it. Water and food. Partners.

The first drop arrived after dark. It carried the chill of the barrel and the faint iron taste of the mountain spring Chen used. It touched Bao's root tip and vanished, pulled inside. Another followed. Then another. The solution was dilute, almost weak by some standards, but for Bao it tasted of patience. Like honey stirred into warm milk, if honey were minerals and milk were groundwater. The water carried the food. The food rode the water. They came as a pair.

*"Oh."*

Bao sighed. His leaves, what few he had, stopped trembling.

*"This. Yes. This I can use."*

Within two weeks, the buds along the slope had changed. Bao's own body swelled, taking on a pale green color that collectors sometimes call "jade snail." None of the leaves showed the brown scorch marks that strong fertilizer leaves when it lands wrong. None of the roots gasped. The tubes didn't rest. They fed at noon when the sun hammered the ridge. They fed at midnight while moths bumped against Chen's porch light. Each plant received what it needed, more or less. The timing was never perfect. But it was close enough.

Harvest arrived on a morning when the fog lingered longer than usual. Master Chen moved down the rows with a wicker basket lined with muslin. His fingers found Bao and pinched, quick and sure. He held the bud up to the light.

*"Look at you,"* Chen said. There was mud on his boots. *"Just look."*

Bao became a white tea, or something very like one. When the hot water hit him in a glass pot, he released a smell reminiscent of rain on slate and young apricots. The taste carried the mineral edge of Misty Peak's soil. As he unfurled, Bao thought of the blue tubes. They hadn't really known anything, of course. They were rubber and pressure and gravity. Yet they had shared. They had cared, in the only way a straw can care—by delivering just enough, and no more, and never alone.

So it goes, still, in the gardens behind Misty Peak. The plants rest when the temperature drops. Perhaps they dream of slow water. Perhaps they don't dream at all. The stars are there regardless, dimmed sometimes by cloud, and the wind moves through the rows with a sound like someone humming half-remembered words.

The end.

*Sleep tight. May your own rest be gentle. Like tea brewed at the right temperature. Like water arriving, finally, where it was needed all along. Goodnight.*

title: The Orchard in Winter
text:
写了一篇英语短文给你参考，结构上是挺经典的那种五段式，议论带点描写：开头一段引言，中间三个主体段，最后收尾。如下：

The Orchard in Winter

Ask most people to picture an orchard and they'll give you autumn, branches heavy with fruit, or maybe spring with everything in blossom. Winter rarely comes up. Fair enough. But I'd argue the winter orchard has a beauty of its own, and a purpose too. Once the leaves and fruit are gone, the trees finally show you what they're made of. The land gets its rest. And the quiet out there has something to teach, mostly about patience. It's not a dead or empty place at all. It's more like a held breath.

The first thing that hits you is the bareness. Stripped of foliage, the trees stand as dark, tangled silhouettes against that flat pale sky, and you notice branch patterns you'd never see in June. Row after row of trunks makes a kind of quiet geometry across the field. When it snows, every limb gets traced in white and the whole orchard turns into a drawing of itself. Frost sits on the bark early in the morning, and the sun, low as it is, throws long blue shadows over the frozen ground. None of this has the easy charm of blossom season. It's austere, honestly. But it pays back anyone willing to slow down and look, because what you're seeing is the structure itself, nothing dressed up, and there's a cleaner beauty in that.

For all that stillness, though, the orchard is nowhere near lifeless. Winter is dormancy, and dormancy is work, just the invisible kind. The trees are conserving energy, getting ready for the push of growth ahead. A lot of fruit trees flat-out need the cold: they require a certain number of "chill hours" before they can blossom at all. Skip the cold winter and you lose the spring bloom, and with it the autumn harvest. The cold does another job too, killing off pests and diseases that would otherwise pile up year after year. And this is when people do their part. Pruning is winter work. Orchardists go out in the cold and cut away the dead or crowded branches, shaping each tree for the season to come. Every cut made in January is money in the bank for September.

There's a symbolic layer to all this, at least for me. The winter orchard keeps insisting that rest is not the same thing as death. Stretches of apparent inactivity are often the most important preparation there is. We live in a culture more or less addicted to constant productivity, and the orchard offers a quiet rebuttal: real growth demands still seasons. Those branches a passerby would dismiss as dead sticks are already carrying next spring's buds, the leaves, the flowers, all of it folded in there. Walking through in the cold months, you can't help thinking about how endings and beginnings are tangled up together, and how hope usually hides just under the surface of things.

So the winter orchard won't hand you ripe fruit or the smell of blossom. What it hands you instead is a picture of resilience: patience, quiet preparation, faith in what's coming. The bare trees argue for structure over surface. The dormancy is a reminder that rest isn't optional. And the buds, tucked away where you'd barely notice them, are a small promise that renewal is already on its way. Anyone who takes the time to look will find the place isn't empty in the slightest. It's waiting, gathering strength for what's next. That's all.
