title: 番茄品质提升与增效途径
text:
The Sweetness of Summer

Twenty years. That was how long Hector Morales had watched his tomatoes shrink—pale and cracked, passed over at the market by buyers who barely glanced up. Valle del Sol had once been known up and down the valley for ruby-red fruit. Now the soil was exhausted, fertilizer costs kept climbing, and the flavor had leached out of the land the way color fades from old cloth.

Then Maria Ortega arrived. She was an agricultural engineer with mud on her boots and a tablet in her backpack. Hector agreed to let her have one hectare. Just one.

“Better tomatoes come from better balance,” she said that first morning. She sampled the soil and found the pH scattered—patches as low as 5.2, others closer to neutral—and organic matter down to almost nothing. She spread compost and rice-hull biochar across the field. Drip-irrigation lines went in, each tied to a soil-moisture sensor that Hector figured would break in the first rain. “Less water,” Maria promised. “Stronger roots. Sweeter fruit.”

Next she replaced Hector’s aging seeds with a hybrid called Solar Fire, chosen mainly for flavor but also because it could stand up to wilt. For the prized heirloom scion he refused to abandon, she taught him grafting: a tough, disease-resistant rootstock below, his beloved top above. They set the young plants into raised beds covered with biodegradable plastic mulch. It held warmth and kept the worst weeds down.

Maria trained Hector’s workers to prune each vine to two main stems, stripping the leafy suckers that stole energy from the fruit. Lower leaves were trimmed to let air move through. Yellow sticky traps caught whiteflies; releases of predatory mites went after spider mites. Hector was surprised. Healthier plants needed fewer spray rounds, not more.

Technology brought a kind of order. Maria set up a simple mobile app to record rainfall and fertilizer applications. Harvest weights went in too. It was clunky. Hector sometimes forgot to enter numbers. Still, a pattern emerged. Too much nitrogen produced jungle-like vines but watery, tasteless tomatoes. Cutting nitrogen back and adding potassium and calcium late in the season deepened the color and kept blossom-end rot at bay. Not every tomato was perfect. Some still rotted. But fewer.

Harvest changed too. Workers used laminated color cards to pick each tomato at its ideal ripeness. Crates waited in the shade. A small optical grader in the new packing shed sorted fruit by size and firmness. The boxes looked uniform. Buyers at the city market paid a premium, and a nearby sauce factory signed a two-season contract.

By August, the trial hectare had produced about twenty percent more fruit than the rest of the farm. The tomatoes were larger and sweeter, and far less of the crop rotted before sale. Neighbors came to see vines heavy with glossy scarlet globes. Eventually the cooperative pooled money for compost and shared sensors, then later for time on the grading machine. Sharing the grader meant scheduling squabbles. But it worked.

At the village harvest festival, a local chef sliced one of Hector’s tomatoes onto warm bread with salt and olive oil. The crowd went quiet. Then someone laughed out loud. The taste was bright, almost honeyed—the kind of summer you cannot fake.

Hector raised his glass to Maria. “You brought the magic back.”

Maria shook her head. “The magic was already here. We just gave it science and patience. A little discipline too.”

As the sun set over Valle del Sol, Hector smiled at rows of red promise. His tomatoes had not only improved; his whole farm had learned to work smarter. And that, he knew, was the sweetest harvest of all.

title: On Books and Firelight
text:
On Books and Firelight: Firelight as a Material, Social, and Imaginative Condition of Reading

---

Abstract

For almost the whole of human history, reading after dark meant reading by firelight. Still, scholarship on books and reading has usually gravitated toward the text, the author, the market, and the reader, leaving light to one side as if it were merely a neutral backdrop. This article makes the case that firelight is not just an obsolete technology of premodern illumination. It is, rather, a material, social, and symbolic condition that helped shape the book as an object and reading as an embodied practice. Drawing together history of the book, media studies, and the environmental humanities, I look at how the hearth organized reading after nightfall, how firelight mediated the passage between oral and literate cultures, and how the flame appears at once as the book’s guardian and its destroyer. Even now, in a time of constant electric and digital light, the fireside book remains a potent image of slowness, intimacy, and fragile memory. To rethink books through firelight is to see reading as situated, sensory, and vulnerable rather than as a purely mental operation.

Keywords: books, firelight, history of reading, materiality, domesticity, orality and literacy, memory, destruction of libraries

---

1. Introduction

Picture the familiar scene: someone alone with a bound volume, face lit by the wavering glow of a hearth. It appears almost everywhere—medieval scriptoria, nineteenth-century parlors, contemporary Instagram posts tagged *hygge*. Books paired with firelight suggest warmth, quiet thought, shelter from the darkness outside. What we rarely stop to ask is how deeply that pairing shaped reading itself. Before gaslight, electric bulbs, and backlit screens, fire was the only way most people could see a page once the sun had set. It therefore decided when, where, how, and with whom people read. Firelight arranged domestic space, governed attention, and gave the book its social meanings.

I want to treat firelight as a serious subject for book history and reading studies. The argument has three strands, each woven through the others. Materially, firelight both limited and enabled reading: its narrow reach, flicker, heat, and danger turned the book into something held close to the body and made reading a slow, concentrated act. Socially and imaginatively, the fireside formed a threshold between oral and literate cultures, a place where stories were told aloud and where silent readers slipped into printed worlds without ever quite leaving the household’s sounds and feelings. Finally, the bond between books and fire is contradictory: the same flame that made reading possible could also turn a library to ash, making the book a token of both preservation and loss. Taken together, these strands imply that the book cannot be separated from the conditions under which it was seen.

The discussion moves through four sections. I begin by reconstructing what it felt like to read by firelight in the preindustrial night. Next I consider the fireside as a social and imaginative chronotope. The third section turns to the other side of the dialectic: book burning and library fires as both historical disasters and symbolic performances. The fourth asks what survives of the book-and-firelight image in an era of ever-present light and digital text. The conclusion reflects on what this history means for contemporary reading and for the environmental and emotional economies of attention.

---

2. The Phenomenology of Nocturnal Reading

In the preindustrial world, night felt like a different country. Historians have shown that darkness was not simply the absence of day but a separate temporal and social realm (Ekirch 2005). Sleep was often “segmented,” split into a first and second sleep with a wakeful interval in between, when people prayed, talked, thought, and sometimes read. During those hours, firelight—from hearth, candle, oil lamp, or rushlight—was the main defense against the dark. Reading by firelight was therefore not a casual afterthought; it belonged to a particular ecology of fuel, flame, body, and page.

The material difficulties were real. Firelight is local and unsteady. Its circle is small; beyond it, things dissolve into shadow. It keeps moving, sending a trembling light across the page that can tire the eyes. Smoke, soot, and smell were ordinary companions of reading. Because candles and oil cost money, reading after dark was often a luxury for those who could afford both light and literacy. For many others, reading happened communally around a single flame, or it did not happen at all. These conditions meant the book had to be drawn near to the body and to the flame. Reading meant leaning in, tilting the page to catch the light, feeling heat on one cheek while the other stayed cool.

This bodily closeness shaped the emotional and cognitive texture of reading. A book under firelight was not one object among many in a bright room; it became the glowing center of a narrow visual field. That intensity favored certain genres and habits of attention—devotional texts, almanacs, letters, novels, poems—forms that could be taken in short stretches or read aloud. The reader’s posture and pace differed from the upright, rapid scanning encouraged by modern electric or digital reading (Crary 1999). Reading by firelight was slow, interrupted, recurrent. One had to tend the fire, trim the wick, answer a voice from the shadows.

Yet firelight also lengthened the day. It made the night usable, turning the hours after sunset into a space for private study, household devotion, or imaginative escape. In this sense, the flame expanded time even as it concentrated space. It allowed the written word to move into the night, though it never let the reader forget the bodily, domestic setting of that movement. The page always hung between light and darkness, between being seen and disappearing.

---

3. The Hearth as Chronotope: Between Orality and Literacy

The fireside is among the oldest of human gathering places. Long before writing, it was where stories were told, rituals performed, and memory passed on. The light pulled faces into a circle and made shared attention possible; the darkness beyond the circle sharpened the feeling that the world of the tale was the only world that mattered. When books entered this space, they did not simply displace oral performance. They complicated it, layered over it, and eventually produced new forms of solitude inside sociability.

Walter Ong’s well-known account of orality and literacy argues that writing restructures consciousness, moving memory away from the embodied, formulaic, and communal toward the analytic, abstract, and individual (Ong 1982). But this shift did not happen overnight, and it did not erase the oral settings in which books were first met. For centuries, books were read aloud around the fire—to families, guests, children. The reader’s voice stood between the silent marks on the page and the listening circle. In this arrangement, the book was at once a solitary artifact and a social tool, something held in the hand and a prompt for collective imagination.

Roger Chartier’s work on reading practices reminds us that the same text can be taken up in radically different ways depending on setting, material form, and social expectation (Chartier 1995). A Bible read aloud by a father after supper was not the same book as that Bible read silently by a scholar in a library. The fireside imposed its own rules: reading was often didactic, devotional, or entertaining; it was woven into the routines of eating, praying, and resting; and it followed the rhythms of the household rather than the abstract schedules of school or workplace.

Mikhail Bakhtin’s concept of the *chronotope*—the inseparable linking of time and space in narrative—offers a useful way to think about the hearth (Bakhtin 1981). The hearth is a chronotope of enclosure: time slows, the outside world withdraws, and the immediate scene grows thick with meaning. A book consumed in this chronotope absorbs those qualities. Nineteenth-century novels, for example, often presented themselves as fireside entertainments, offering the reader a temporary retreat from public life into domestic feeling. Leah Price has shown that in Victorian Britain books were not merely read but displayed, handled, given as gifts, and performed within the rituals of the middle-class home (Price 2012).

title: 白菜种植增收增产技术分析
text:
Reflections on "Technical Analysis of Increasing Income and Yield in Chinese Cabbage Cultivation"

Recently I read *Technical Analysis of Increasing Income and Yield in Chinese Cabbage Cultivation*. The study looks at how farmers can actually make more money growing Chinese cabbage, not just harvest bigger heads. It refuses to stay purely in the realm of agronomy. Economics matter here too. What struck me was how the authors bridge field science with the reality of market prices. This isn't a simple how-to pamphlet. It reshaped how I think about modern vegetable production, particularly for crops that dominate local diets but rarely get analytical treatment this thorough.

The systems-based approach stuck with me. The authors never pretend you can fix yield by tweaking one input alone. Better seed helps. But without matching soil conditions? Limited effect. Water matters too, yet timing changes everything. I found the section on precision water-fertilizer integration especially useful. The idea is straightforward: feed roots directly, stage by stage, rather than broadcasting nutrients across entire fields. In practice, this means drip lines or localized irrigation matched to cabbage development—from rosette formation through head enlargement. Less waste. Lower runoff. Though I wondered whether the upfront tubing costs might scare off some growers, at least the logic holds. Sustainable intensification beats simply planting more acres.

The economics section carries real weight. High yield can still mean lousy returns. That gap gets ignored in too many agricultural papers. The authors look at cost structures, but they also push further. They ask when the cabbage hits market. A January harvest in northern China commands entirely different prices than an August glut. Farmers who track regional consumption patterns and plan accordingly do better. This turns cultivation into something closer to supply-chain management. You need dirt under your fingernails. You also need spreadsheets.

The tone stays practical throughout. Large industrial operations with automated greenhouses aren't the only audience. The authors spend time on techniques that work for smallholders. They suggest adjusting planting densities to match actual land size rather than copying blanket recommendations. Crop rotation comes up as a way to break pest cycles without expensive chemicals. I was glad to see biological controls mentioned too—specifically Trichogramma wasps against cabbage worms. These aren't silver bullets. Weather interferes. Labor availability fluctuates. Still, the emphasis on accessible innovation matters. Technical progress should help ordinary farmers, not just widen the gap between them and corporate farms.

Reading this shifted something for me. The future of farming isn't about longer hours in the field. It's about sharper decisions. The authors manage to keep science and profit in view without letting either frame dominate ecology. That balance helps students think more clearly while giving practitioners something they can use immediately. A policymaker reading this would notice the emphasis on livelihoods rather than raw tonnage. Sustainable advancement means farmers actually keep more money at the end of the season, not just push higher yields through exhausted soil. I'll carry that lens into my own work. Knowledge applied poorly stays theoretical. Applied well, it changes what a field can produce—and who benefits.

title: 三个火枪手
text:
[Journal of Nineteenth-Century European Literature, Vol. XX, No. X, pp. XX–XX]

---

"All for One, One for All": Friendship, Honor, and the Historical Imagination in Alexandre Dumas's *The Three Musketeers*

[Author Name]
[Department of French Literature, University Name]

---

Abstract

This paper reads Alexandre Dumas's *The Three Musketeers* (1844) as a representative product of the French historical novel's golden age. Working from close readings set against historical context, I argue that Dumas takes the raw stuff of seventeenth-century history and remakes it into a romance of male fellowship, one whose ideological center is the famous motto "all for one, one for all." The discussion begins by placing the novel within the craze for historical fiction in post-Revolutionary France and looking at Dumas's collaborative working method. From there it turns to the quartet of heroes as a case study in collective identity, to the uneasy contest between personal honor and state power figured in Cardinal Richelieu, and finally to the novel's gender politics as crystallized in Milady de Winter. The book's lasting hold on readers, I suggest, comes from the way it weds aristocratic adventure to an essentially democratic ideal of loyalty—even as its handling of female agency shows where that ideal runs out.

Keywords: Alexandre Dumas; *The Three Musketeers*; historical novel; French Romanticism; friendship; gender

---

1. Introduction

Hardly any nineteenth-century novel can match the worldwide reach and staying power of Alexandre Dumas's *Les Trois Mousquetaires*. When it appeared in installments in *Le Siècle* between March and July 1844, readers devoured it, and it has never been out of print since. Translations, sequels, stage versions, films—the list goes on (Hemmings). And yet, perhaps precisely because so many people have loved it, scholars have often waved the book aside as light entertainment. That dismissal, I want to argue here, misses something important. The novel works through questions of history, ethics, and social identity with real sophistication. It is not simply an adventure yarn: it builds a coherent moral world around the principle of collective loyalty, while at the same time laying bare the friction between personal honor and raison d'état, and between male solidarity and female agency.

2. Sources and Method: History as a "Nail"

Dumas liked to joke that history served him as "a nail on which I hang my picture," and few of his books illustrate the quip better than this one (Schopp). The premise came from Gatien de Courtilz de Sandras's pseudo-historical *Mémoires de M. d'Artagnan* (1700), which supplied the names Athos, Porthos, and Aramis, along with the Gascon hero himself. The business of the queen's diamond studs, meanwhile, grew out of an anecdote in La Rochefoucauld's memoirs about Anne of Austria and the Duke of Buckingham (Stowe). Working hand in glove with his assistant Auguste Maquet, Dumas took these scattered odds and ends and transformed them wholesale, spinning invented escapades around the documented scaffolding of the siege of La Rochelle and Richelieu's rise to power.

This way of working puts Dumas squarely in the historical novel tradition that Georg Lukács traced back to Walter Scott, though with a distinctly French twist. Scott's protagonists tend to be moderates squeezed between contending historical forces; d'Artagnan is anything but moderate—an active, frequently reckless agent who makes events do his bidding. As Maurice Samuels has shown, France in the 1830s and 1840s was gripped by a genuine "historical fever," and the novel became the chief arena in which a public still digesting the Revolution sorted out its feelings about the national past. What Dumas managed was to open this form up to the feuilleton-reading masses without flattening the storytelling.

3. "All for One": The Ethics of Collective Friendship

The whole moral architecture of the book rests on how the famous quartet comes together. Notably, d'Artagnan's entry into the group begins as farce: fresh off the road from Gascony, he somehow contrives to schedule duels with all three musketeers for the same afternoon. The quarrel melts into alliance once the four find themselves fighting side by side against the Cardinal's guards, and that scene sets the template for everything that follows—hostility flipped into fellowship through combat shared (Dumas, ch. 5).

Each of the four stands for a recognizable ethical type. Athos is the melancholy aristocrat, a Comte de la Fère nursing a buried wound behind his assumed name. Porthos, vain and physically exuberant, turns out to be loyal to the bone. Aramis can never quite decide between the cassock and the world. And d'Artagnan, quick-witted in the way of Gascons, supplies the consciousness that knits the group together. What matters is that their friendship ignores rank: the penniless provincial becomes the full equal of the disguised nobleman. For Dumas's bourgeois readers this was a deeply attractive, even meritocratic fantasy. The motto "tous pour un, un pour tous" operates as a kind of voluntary social contract—a private polity that proves far more dependable than the corrupt institutions of court and church the novel puts on display (Bell).

4. Honor, Service, and the State

Set against this private ethics of friendship stands the impersonal machinery of the state, given human form in Cardinal Richelieu. Dumas handles the Cardinal with surprising evenhandedness. Richelieu engineers the novel's central conspiracy and uses Milady as his instrument, yet he never shrinks into a cardboard villain. His grudging respect for d'Artagnan, which peaks in the lieutenancy he hands over at the end, hints that Dumas saw a kindred spirit in him: one more self-made man bending history to his purposes (Hemmings).

The siege of La Rochelle is where private adventure and public history actually collide. The musketeers chase their personal vendetta against Milady while, all around them, the fate of French Protestantism is being settled once and for all. Dumas surely means this juxtaposition. He leaves his readers wondering whether the heroes' code of personal loyalty offers a refuge from the pitiless logic of state-building that Richelieu embodies—or a quiet commentary on it.

5. Milady de Winter: Gender, Agency, and Punishment

Nobody can read this novel seriously and skip over Milady de Winter, arguably the most complicated character Dumas ever created. Her intelligence outstrips that of the four heroes again and again; yet the narrative installs her as absolute evil, branded with the fleur-de-lis, criminality written into her very flesh. The climax at Armentières—where the four musketeers, Lord de Winter, and the executioner of Lille convene what amounts to an extralegal court to try her and put her to death—has made readers uneasy since the book first appeared (Dumas, ch. 65–66).

Looked at through a feminist lens, the episode becomes an act of patriarchal violence aimed at female agency as such. Milady's real crime, at bottom, is her refusal to stay inside the parts allotted to her: wife, widow, subordinate. The fact that the heroes must pool their masculine authority to destroy a single woman tells us something about how fragile the celebrated fellowship actually is. Recent adaptations have leaned into this ambiguity more and more, presenting Milady as a proto-feminist figure crushed by a homosocial order—and in doing so they bring to the surface tensions that were there in Dumas's pages all along (Schopp).

6. Serialization, Reception, and Afterlife

The shape of the novel owes a great deal to the conditions under which it was produced. It came out as a *roman-feuilleton* in Émile de Girardin's *Le Siècle*, the paper that pioneered the cheap mass-circulation press, and Dumas composed it in installments whose cliffhangers and rhythmic climaxes still drive the narrative today. The gamble paid off handsomely—subscriptions reportedly jumped—and the success fixed the serial as the dominant literary form of mid-century France, with Dumas himself becoming the prototype of the modern bestselling author (Stowe).

What happened afterward is just as striking. English and dozens of other translations followed almost at once; stage versions appeared within a few years of publication; the book has been filmed more than forty times since the silent era. *The Three Musketeers* has turned into a global myth of friendship. The two sequels, *Twenty Years After* and *The Vicomte de Bragelonne*, stretched the saga across the heroes' whole lives, yet it is the first book's picture of four inseparable comrades that has proved genuinely universal.

7. Conclusion

*The Three Musketeers* lasts because it pulls off a delicate ideological balancing act. It gives readers the glamour of aristocratic adventure while quietly preaching a thoroughly modern gospel of loyalty among equals. The musketeers' world looks backward, to the age of the sword and the code duello, but the ethics of that world—merit rewarded, rank set aside, a promise kept whatever it costs—spoke directly to the bourgeois nineteenth century and still speak now. At the same time, the novel cannot entirely hide the costs of its own ideal. The trial of Milady shows what the fellowship is prepared to do, and to whom, when its solidarity feels threatened. Readers who find the book merely charming are not looking closely enough; those who find it merely reactionary are not looking closely either. The truth lies in the tension—and that, more than the swordplay, is why we keep reading.

text:
Phased Implementation Checklist: Key Technologies for Dairy Cow Facility Management  
*A hands-on, step-by-step guide to designing, building, and running a modern dairy facility*

---

 1. Pre-Project Planning & Feasibility

|   | Task | Target / What Counts as Done |
|---|------|------------------------------|
| ☐ | 1.1 Site selection | Flat or gently sloping ground (<3%); within 2 km of a paved road; reliable grid power plus backup generator capacity; enough water (≥100 L/cow/day); manure-disposal land base of at least 5–10 ha per 100 cows. |
| ☐ | 1.2 Environmental impact screening | Secure permits for waste storage, discharge, odor, and animal welfare; prepare a nutrient-management plan; respect setback distances from watercourses and dwellings under local rules. |
| ☐ | 1.3 Herd-size decision | Set final capacity (for example, 500 lactating cows plus 20% young stock) and design for 120% of that target so there is room to grow and add separation pens. |
| ☐ | 1.4 Technology selection workshop | Pick housing (freestall or loose housing), the milking system (herringbone, parallel, or rotary), manure handling (scrape, flush, or flush + separator), cooling, feeding, and a digital monitoring platform. |
| ☐ | 1.5 Budget & procurement plan | Allow contingencies of roughly 60% for construction, 30% for equipment, and 10% for commissioning and training. |

---

 2. Facility Design & Engineering

 2.1 Building Layout

|   | Task | Target / What Counts as Done |
|---|------|------------------------------|
| ☐ | 2.1.1 Freestall dimensions | 1.15–1.20 m wide and 1.70–1.80 m long per Holstein cow, adjusted for breed size; brisket board 10–15 cm high and 1.60 m from the rear curb. |
| ☐ | 2.1.2 Stocking density | No more than 100% in lactating pens, 85% in transition/dry pens, and 100% in hospital/withdrawal pens—avoid overcrowding. |
| ☐ | 2.1.3 Feed-bunk space | At least 60 cm of linear bunk space per lactating cow; 70 cm or more for transition cows; feed lane at least 4.0 m wide. |
| ☐ | 2.1.4 Water access | One trough per 15–20 cows; linear drinking space ≥5 cm/cow; flow rate ≥15 L/min; summer water temperature ≤25 °C. |
| ☐ | 2.1.5 Alley widths | Feed alley 3.6–4.2 m; scrape alley 2.4–3.0 m; holding area 1.2–1.5 m²/cow; exit lanes 3.0–4.0 m wide. |

 2.2 Ventilation & Cooling

|   | Task | Target / What Counts as Done |
|---|------|------------------------------|
| ☐ | 2.2.1 Natural ventilation design | Continuous ridge opening ≥5 cm per 3 m of building width; sidewall opening ≥2% of floor area; curtains motorized and wind-rated. |
| ☐ | 2.2.2 Mechanical ventilation backup | Tunnel or cross ventilation able to deliver 4–6 air changes/hour in winter and 40–60 in summer; summer airspeed at cow level 1.5–2.5 m/s. |
| ☐ | 2.2.3 Feedline soaking system | Soaker nozzles every 1.8–2.0 m above the feed bunk; cycle 180 s on / 1,200 s off when THI >68; water use ≤1.5 L/cow/hour. |
| ☐ | 2.2.4 Circulation fans | 1.2 m diameter fans on a 6 m × 6 m grid in holding and lying areas; automated via temperature/THI sensors; use VFDs where practical. |
| ☐ | 2.2.5 Shade structures | 70–80% shade cloth over exercise lots; orient east–west where possible. |

 2.3 Flooring & Bedding

|   | Task | Target / What Counts as Done |
|---|------|------------------------------|
| ☐ | 2.3.1 Flooring choices | Grooved concrete in alleys (2 cm wide × 2 cm deep grip grooves, 10 cm apart); rubber mats or cushions in holding areas and parlour return alleys. |
| ☐ | 2.3.2 Bedding selection | Sand is ideal—25–30 kg/stall/week. Alternatives: kiln-dried recycled manure solids (<40% moisture) or straw at ≥5 kg/cow/day. |
| ☐ | 2.3.3 Stall base | Deep-bedded sand 15–20 cm, or a mattress with ≥5 cm bedding; target hock-lesion prevalence below 10%. |

 2.4 Manure & Waste Management

|   | Task | Target / What Counts as Done |
|---|------|------------------------------|
| ☐ | 2.4.1 Collection frequency | Scrape alleys 2–3 times a day; size flush systems for at least two daily flushes. |
| ☐ | 2.4.2 Storage capacity | Liquid manure storage for ≥180 days (or local regulatory minimum); lined lagoons/pits; cover or install a solid separator. |
| ☐ | 2.4.3 Solid-liquid separation | Screw press or roller separator; separated solids reach 18–20% dry matter for bedding or composting. |
| ☐ | 2.4.4 Biogas feasibility (optional) | For herds above 300 cows, evaluate an anaerobic digester; target ≥60% methane capture; digestate storage ≥90 days. |

 2.5 Milking Parlour & Milk Handling

|   | Task | Target / What Counts as Done |
|---|------|------------------------------|
| ☐ | 2.5.1 Parlour sizing | Finish milking each group within 2.5–3.0 hours; 1.2–1.5 milking units per 10 cows (for example, a 2×12 parlour for about 200 cows). |
| ☐ | 2.5.2 Vacuum & pulsation | System vacuum 42–44 kPa (low line) or 48–50 kPa (high line); pulsation ratio 60:40 or 65:35; automatic cluster removal on every unit. |
| ☐ | 2.5.3 Milk cooling | Plate cooler plus bulk tank; cool milk to ≤4 °C within two hours of milking; tank capacity ≥1 day’s production plus 20%. |
| ☐ | 2.5.4 CIP & hygiene | Full CIP after every milking: warm-water rinse, alkaline wash at 75 °C, acid wash every other day; ATP swabs below 200 RLU weekly. |

 2.6 Feed & Nutrition System

|   | Task | Target / What Counts as Done |
|---|------|------------------------------|
| ☐ | 2.6.1 TMR mixer | Sized for the largest ration batch; mixing error ≤5%; weigh cells calibrated monthly. |
| ☐ | 2.6.2 Feed storage | Silage bunkers, bags, or piles sized for 6–12 months; feed mill/hay shed protected from rain; ingredient bays kept separate. |
| ☐ | 2.6.3 Feed delivery | Fresh TMR delivered once daily; feed pushed up every two hours during the day; refusal target 3–5% of offered feed. |
| ☐ | 2.6.4 Particle length audit | Penn State Particle Separator: >19 mm at 3–8%; 8–19 mm at 45–55%; <8 mm at 40–50%; check weekly. |

 2.7 Water, Power & Biosecurity Infrastructure

|   | Task | Target / What Counts as Done |
|---|------|------------------------------|
| ☐ | 2.7.1 Water system | On-farm water storage for 2–3 days; test quarterly for bacteria and chemicals; chlorinate if coliforms exceed 10 CFU/100 mL. |
| ☐ | 2.7.2 Backup power | Generator capacity ≥120% of critical load (milking, ventilation, feed mixer, water pumps); automatic transfer switch; test run monthly. |
| ☐ | 2.7.3 Perimeter biosecurity | 2.0 m perimeter fence; single controlled entrance; vehicle dip or foam at the gate; visitor log and restricted zones. |

---

 3. Construction & Installation

|   | Task | Target / What Counts as Done |
|---|------|------------------------------|
| ☐ | 3.1 Civil works | Complete foundations, floors, drainage slopes (1.5–2% toward channels), pits, and retaining walls; cure and seal concrete. |
| ☐ | 3.2 Steel/building envelope | Roof and walls watertight; ridge and sidewall openings match approved drawings; install and test curtains and motors. |
| ☐ | 3.3 Electrical & control wiring | All sensors, VFDs, lighting, and emergency circuits installed; lighting ≥200 lux at feed bunk and parlour, ≥50 lux in alleys. |
| ☐ | 3.4 Plumbing & cooling lines | Pressure-test soaker lines at ≥3 bar; size drains for peak flow; fit non-return valves and backflow prevention. |
| ☐ | 3.5 Equipment delivery & positioning | Place and anchor milking equipment, TMR mixer, scrapers/robots, separators, and generators per manufacturer specifications. |
| ☐ | 3.6 Pre-commissioning inspection | Close out punch-list; install safety guards; verify emergency stops; provide fire extinguishers and first-aid stations. |

---

 4. Commissioning & Pre-Operation

|   | Task | Target / What Counts as Done |
|---|------|------------------------------|
| ☐ | 4.1 Ventilation testing | Measure airspeed at cow level in every pen; confirm minimum winter air exchange and summer cooling velocities. |
| ☐ | 4.2 Soaker & fan calibration | Verify nozzle flow uniformity (±10%); confirm THI trigger setpoints and timer cycles. |
| ☐ | 4.3 Milking system validation | Vacuum stability within ±1 kPa; inspect pulsation charts; adjust ACR settings; calibrate milk meters against known volumes. |
| ☐ | 4.4 CIP verification | Run a full CIP cycle; rinse water pH neutral; pass ATP swabs; log bulk-tank cooling curve. |
| ☐ | 4.5 Feed system calibration | Zero/span check on TMR mixer weigh cells; verify ingredient discharge rates; mix and sample a test ration. |
| ☐ | 4.6 Manure system trials | Run scrapers, flush pumps, and separator for 48 hours; inspect drainage, sump levels, and overflow paths. |
| ☐ | 4.7 Digital monitoring platform | Connect RFID readers, activity/rumination collars, environmental sensors, milk meters, and cameras; dashboard shows real-time alerts. |
| ☐ | 4.8 Staff training | Train all operators on SOPs for milking, heat detection, calving, lameness, feed mixing, CIP, and emergency shutdown; file sign-off sheets. |
| ☐ | 4.9 Biosecurity activation | Set up footbaths filled with 5% copper sulfate or an approved alternative at parlour |

title: 西游记
text:
The Pilgrimage as Compromise: Narrative, Religion, and Bureaucracy in *Journey to the West*

---

 Abstract

Most readings of *Journey to the West* want to know whether the book is Buddhist allegory, Daoist satire, or popular entertainment pretending to be both. I sidestep that choice. My narrower claim is that the novel’s hundred-chapter pilgrimage advances through repeated local bargains rather than through the steady spiritual conversion of its characters. Sun Wukong is tamed not because he sees the truth but because the celestial administration finds a use for him; the demons are usually reabsorbed into the pantheon rather than destroyed. Working with the 1592 printed text conventionally attributed to Wu Cheng’en, and treating its religious language as narrative material rather than as doctrine, I argue that the text’s real subject is the conversion of conflict into detachable episodes. The argument is limited to narrative structure and does not explain the novel’s humor, its complicated textual history, or the religious beliefs of Ming readers.

Keywords: *Journey to the West*, Wu Cheng’en, Ming vernacular fiction, pilgrimage narrative, Sun Wukong, narrative structure

---

 1. Where the Argument Starts

*Journey to the West* has a reputation problem. It is too long, too repetitive, too silly, and too sacred. Critics who want to elevate it call it allegory; critics who want to defend its vulgarity call it subversive. Both sides assume the novel must finally mean one thing. I think it means several things at once, and that this instability is built into the plot itself.

The pilgrims do not change much. Tripitaka remains frightened; Zhu Bajie remains greedy; Sha Wujing remains so thinly drawn that a reader can forget he is there. Yet the novel keeps moving. Why? Because each chapter renegotiates the same practical question: who has the authority to delay, obstruct, or expedite the journey west? The answer is almost always a bureaucrat with a past.

My argument depends on a few assumptions that should be stated plainly. First, I treat the 1592 printed text as the object of analysis and attribute it, conventionally, to Wu Cheng’en. I am aware that the authorship is disputed, but the dispute matters more for reception history than for what I am doing here. Second, I read the novel as a finished literary artifact, not as a transcript of oral storytelling or as a repository of religious doctrine. Third, I use the English word “demon” loosely, as a translation of *yaoguai* and related terms, while recognizing that the translation flattions distinctions a Ming reader might have felt. These assumptions restrict the scope of what follows. I am talking about narrative mechanics, not about the history of Chinese Buddhism, the Yuan-period *zaju* antecedents, or the global afterlife of Monkey in manga and television.

---

 2. The Episodic Structure as Argument

The novel’s plot is famously repetitive. The pilgrims arrive somewhere. A demon captures Tripitaka. Sun Wukong fights, loses, seeks help from a god or bodhisattva, and discovers that the demon is the runaway servant, pet, or relative of a higher power. The demon is repatriated, not killed, and the journey resumes.

This is not merely a formula. It is the novel’s argument. The monsters are not random eruptions of evil; they are displaced fragments of the same hierarchy the pilgrims supposedly serve. Red Boy, for example, is the son of Princess Iron Fan and the Bull Demon King, and after his defeat Guanyin takes him on as an attendant (Yu, 1977–1983, Vol. 2). The two boys at Golden Horn and Silver Horn turn out to be Laozi’s servants (Yu, 1977–1983, Vol. 1). The monstrous kings at Lion Camel Ridge have ties to the Buddha and to Manjusri. Even the flesh-eating villains are, in a sense, employees who have wandered off the job.

What this means is that violence in the novel is outsourced and then recalled. The pantheon is absolute in theory and leaky in practice. Each episode therefore resolves not by destroying evil but by restoring paperwork. Sun Wukong does not defeat demons so much as he returns them to their proper files.

This reading has a limit. It does not mean the novel is cynical about religion. Many chapters contain straightforward sermons on karma, emptiness, and merit. The point is simpler: the *plot* is organized around administrative repair, not around inner transformation.

---

 3. Monkey as Employee, Not Saint

Sun Wukong’s arc looks like conversion. He begins as a rebellious stone monkey, makes havoc in heaven, is imprisoned under Five Elements Mountain, and is released to serve Tripitaka. By the end he is awarded the title Buddha of Victorious Strife. But the change is more institutional than spiritual.

After his release, Monkey is still violent, impatient, and opportunistic. He kills robbers, threatens monks, and tries to solve every problem by hitting it. What has changed is that he now has a manager. The golden headband is not a symbol of enlightenment; it is a device of remote discipline. Tripitaka recites the tightening spell, and Monkey obeys. Their relationship is a comedy of mutual incomprehension, but it is also a labor contract.

Monkey’s real skill is not meditation. It is bureaucracy. He knows the names of local gods, the jurisdictions of heavenly departments, and the proper forms of appeal. When a demon is too strong, he does not pray; he files a complaint. The novel therefore presents spiritual progress as a series of successful interventions in a celestial civil service.

Tripitaka, meanwhile, is necessary precisely because he is useless in a fight. His vulnerability generates the obstacles. Without a monk who can be kidnapped, boiled, or married against his will, there is no story. His fear is not a flaw to be overcome; it is a narrative resource.

---

 4. Hypothetical Examples

To make the structural argument concrete, I want to test it against three hypothetical cases. These are not claims about what “really” happens in the text. They are thought experiments designed to show what the plot assumes.

Hypothetical Example 1: A demon with no patron.  
Suppose a *yaoguai* appears who is genuinely independent, with no connection to a god, bodhisattva, or immortal. In the novel, such demons are usually killed outright or dispatched without ceremony. Nameless mountain spirits and river monsters die by the dozens. The demons who survive are the ones who can be sent back to their masters. This suggests that survival in the novel depends less on morality than on documentation. A monster with a file gets reassigned; a monster without one gets destroyed.

Hypothetical Example 2: An invulnerable Tripitaka.  
Imagine that the Tang monk could not be captured, seduced, or cooked. The pilgrimage would be shorter. It would also be uninteresting. Tripitaka’s helplessness is not simply a virtue; it is a structural device that creates the need for Sun Wukong’s interventions, Zhu Bajie’s failures, and the interventions of divine bureaucracy. Without his repeated capture, the episodic engine stalls.

Hypothetical Example 3: Early enlightenment.  
Suppose Sun Wukong achieves Buddhahood in chapter 30. The remaining seventy chapters would be redundant. The novel formally treats deliverance as an end-of-narrative reward, not as a present experience. This is not necessarily a theological statement about Buddhism; it is a constraint of the pilgrimage form. Once the characters are fully transformed, the story has nowhere to go.

These examples are assumptions, not proofs. They illustrate what the plot takes for granted.

---

 5. What the Argument Cannot Do

I have been arguing that *Journey to the West* converts conflict into episodes and that its characters are functions of a bureaucratic plot machine. That argument leaves a great deal unexplained.

It does not explain the novel’s humor, which often depends on bodily appetite, wordplay, and the gap between sacred language and profane behavior. It does not explain the social satire directed at judges, monks, and emperors. It does not explain the rich local detail of each episode, which sometimes seems to exist for its own pleasure. And it does not settle the question of authorship or the relationship between the printed novel and earlier dramatic and storytelling traditions.

There is also a translation problem. English versions by Anthony Yu and W. J. F. Jenner are excellent, but they must render terms like *fo*, *xian*, *yao*, and *gui* into a Christianized vocabulary of Buddha, immortal, and demon. My analysis relies on those translations while knowing they are approximations. A reader working in Chinese may see distinctions I have blurred.

Finally, my claim is provisional. I am saying that one way to read the novel’s structure is as a system for managing contradiction. I am not saying this is the only way, or the deepest.

---

 Conclusion

What I have tried to show is that *Journey to the West* is less interested in arrival than in the machinery of delay. The pilgrims reach India because the text keeps finding ways to turn obstacles back into the system that produced them. Sun Wukong becomes useful not because he stops being a monster but because the heavens learn to employ him. The demons are rarely annihilated because annihilation would waste a good resource.

The novel is a compromise. It wants spiritual aspiration and narrative appetite at the same time, and it solves the tension by making the pilgrimage an endless administrative negotiation. We keep reading, perhaps, not to see characters transformed but to see how the next crisis will be folded back into the familiar order. That is not a grand conclusion. It is, I think, enough.

---

title: 中药材产业发展现状与对策
text:
The Planting End

My uncle grows honeysuckle in Shandong. Two acres. Last year the price dropped to eight yuan per kilo, which didn't cover the picking cost, so he let half of it rot on the vines. This year the price hit forty. He planted more. Everyone did. That is the first problem.

Chinese medicinal materials, the zhongyicai industry, runs on millions of uncles making separate guesses. In Anhui they plant peony root. In Yunnan, Paris polyphylla. In Sichuan, ligusticum. The maps look organized if you read the provincial reports. On the ground it is fragment sprayed across hillsides. A farmer in Gansu switches from astragalus to qianghuo because a cousin heard a rumor from a buyer in Chengdu. No one checks soil suitability. The county agricultural bureau hands out pamphlets that dissolve in the rain.

Quality follows from this chaos. In the large wholesale markets, Bozhou or Anguo, you can smell the sulfur before you see the bulbs. Dried tangerine peel bright orange. Angelica slices too white. The old processing methods required patience—drying ginger in shade, slicing licorice after the right number of frost days. Now they bake everything fast and bleach what turns brown. Laboratories in Japan and Hong Kong keep finding heavy metals in shipped roots, pesticide residues in chrysanthemum flowers. The EU updated its limits in 2023. Our exports didn't grow; they shrank slightly, though the government report uses a different quarter to hide this.

Price fluctuation eats the profits before anyone can reinvest. Look at rhubarb, dahuan. In 2019 it was twenty yuan a kilogram at the Chengdu market. By 2021 it hit seventy. Farmers tore up corn to plant rhubarb. Now it is back to thirty-five. The speculators in the Bozhou warehouses make money either way. They stack burlap bags in climate-controlled rooms and release them when clinics panic. The farmer who dug the hole gets nothing from that margin. Some counties tried price insurance. Bureaucrats filled out forms. The payouts arrived six months late, if at all.

Modernization efforts exist. They just don't fit the dirt. A company in Zhejiang built a traceability system where every bag of fritillaria gets a QR code. You scan it and see the mountain, the harvest date, the test results. It worked for their own five hundred mu. The neighboring farms forged the codes with printers bought online. A traceability chain is only as strong as the farmer who bothers to charge his phone. Another province handed out smartphones to cooperative leaders. Three months later half were broken, half were used only for TikTok.

Research looks good on paper. The Chinese Academy of Traditional Chinese Medicine publishes thousands of articles on active compounds, genomics, extraction efficiency. Walk into the seed stores in Tongling and ask for a certified disease-free cultivar of salvia. The clerk shrugs. He has the same seeds his grandfather had, mixed with red bean seeds from the sack next door. The gap between journal impact factor and field reality is maybe ten years. Probably fifteen.

What actually helps, where I have seen it, is when a processing factory moves into the county and signs a contract directly. Not a vague "cooperative" with a banner and a handshake, but a floor price written down, a technician who visits twice a month to check pesticide logs, a drying facility the farmers can use for a fee. In one county in Shanxi this happened with codonopsis. The defect rate dropped. The farmers stopped spraying randomly because the technician explained, in dialect, that the buyer rejected the last truck for excessive pyrethroids. Simple. Specific. Boring. It doesn't scale easily because each county grows different things and each dialect requires a different technician.

Policy keeps pushing for industrial clusters, for "international standards," for digital agriculture platforms. The platforms look beautiful on urban screens. Meanwhile the Bozhou market still operates at four in the morning under bare bulbs, buyers rubbing slices of atractylodes between their fingers to guess the oil content by smell. That expertise is real. It is also dying. The young people left for Hefei, for Shenzhen. Who remains to sort the good fritillaria from the sulfur-soaked stuff? Women over sixty, mostly.

Exports won't fix this alone. We keep hoping the West will discover TCM and buy our materials in bulk. They discover it, then they regulate it. German importers want batch consistency that a hillside plot in Guizhou cannot promise. Korean red ginseng sells at a premium because Korea built the brand first, built the story, built the sterile processing plants. Our ginseng is often better. It sells cheaper because the buyer assumes contamination until proven otherwise.

Some fixes are obvious and hard. Stop subsidizing acreage and start subsidizing laboratories at the county level where a farmer can test his soil for cadmium before he plants. Punish sulfur bleaching at the market gate, not with fines that are cheaper than the chemical cost. Let the price speculators pay a holding tax on warehoused materials so they cannot afford to sit on ten tons of astragalus for eighteen months. Train the technicians in dialect. Accept that one province's solution fails in another because the humidity is different, the dialect is different, the root is different.

My uncle didn't check a price forecast. He checked his neighbor. That is the system we have. Changing it means building something that reaches the two-acre plot, the burlap sack, the back of a motorcycle bouncing down a mountain track. Anything else is just noise from the city.
